chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body

sections.heading: Culpable homicide
sections.text: Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.
ingredients: Causing death of a person
By doing an act
With intention of causing death; OR
With intention of causing bodily injury likely to cause death; OR
With knowledge that the act is likely to cause death

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause death
Intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death
Knowledge that the act is likely to cause death

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A lays sticks and turf over a pit, with the intention of thereby causing death, or with the knowledge that death is likely to be thereby caused. Z, believing the ground to be firm, treads on it, falls in and is killed. A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
illustrations.key_principle: Laying a death trap with intention or knowledge of likely death constitutes culpable homicide even without direct physical contact.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A knows Z to be behind a bush. B does not know it. A, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely to cause Z's death, induces B to fire at the bush. B fires and kills Z. Here B may be guilty of no offence; but A has committed the offence of culpable homicide.
illustrations.verdict: A = culpable homicide; B = possibly no offence
illustrations.key_principle: The person with the guilty mind (A) is liable even when the physical act is performed by an innocent agent (B) who lacks mens rea.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, by shooting at a fowl with intent to kill and steal it, kills B, who is behind a bush; A not knowing that he was there. Here, although A was doing an unlawful act, he was not guilty of culpable homicide, as he did not intend to kill B, or to cause death by doing an act that he knew was likely to cause death.
illustrations.key_principle: Mere commission of an unlawful act is insufficient — the specific mens rea (intention or knowledge of likely death) must be present.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A person who causes bodily injury to another who is labouring under a disorder, disease or bodily infirmity, and thereby accelerates the death of that other, shall be deemed to have caused his death.
explanations.plain_language: If the victim had a pre-existing condition and the injury accelerated death, the accused is still deemed to have caused the death.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Where death is caused by bodily injury, the person who causes such bodily injury shall be deemed to have caused the death, although by resorting to proper remedies and skilful treatment the death might have been prevented.
explanations.plain_language: The fact that proper medical treatment could have saved the victim is no defence — causation is still attributed to the accused.

explanations.label: Explanation 3
explanations.text: The causing of the death of a child in the mother's womb is not homicide. But it may amount to culpable homicide to cause the death of a living child, if any part of that child has been brought forth, though the child may not have breathed or been completely born.
explanations.plain_language: Killing a foetus in utero is not homicide; but killing a partially delivered child (even before breathing or complete birth) can be culpable homicide.

sections.heading: Murder
sections.text: Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or—
sections.general_rule: Culpable homicide is murder unless it falls within one of the five exceptions listed below.

clauses_elevating_to_murder.text: If the act by which death is caused is done with the intention of causing death.
If it is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused.
If it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

If the person committing the act knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death, or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as aforesaid.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A shoots Z with the intention of killing him. Z dies in consequence. A commits murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Direct intention to kill + death = murder.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, knowing that Z is labouring under such a disease that a blow is likely to cause his death, strikes him with the intention of causing bodily injury. Z dies in consequence of the blow. A is guilty of murder, although the blow might not have been sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause the death of a person in a sound state of health. But if A, not knowing that Z is labouring under any disease, gives him such a blow as would not in the ordinary course of nature kill a person in a sound state of health, here A, although he may intend to cause bodily injury, is not guilty of murder, if he did not intend to cause death, or such bodily injury as in the ordinary course of nature would cause death.
illustrations.verdict: Murder (if A knew of disease) / Not murder (if A did not know)
illustrations.key_principle: Subjective knowledge of the victim's vulnerability is decisive — the accused is judged on what they actually knew.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A intentionally gives Z a sword-cut or club-wound sufficient to cause the death of a man in the ordinary course of nature. Z dies in consequence. Here A is guilty of murder, although he may not have intended to cause Z's death.
illustrations.key_principle: Intention to inflict a wound that is objectively sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature is sufficient — no need to prove intent to kill.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A without any excuse fires a loaded cannon into a crowd of persons and kills one of them. A is guilty of murder, although he may not have had a premeditated design to kill any particular individual.
illustrations.key_principle: Knowledge of imminently dangerous act + commission without excuse = murder even without targeting a specific victim.

exceptions.heading: Grave and Sudden Provocation
exceptions.text: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident.

provisos.text: The provocation is not sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for killing or doing harm to any person.
The provocation is not given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant in the lawful exercise of the powers of such public servant.
The provocation is not given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence.

exceptions.explanation: Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to prevent the offence from amounting to murder is a question of fact.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, under the influence of passion excited by a provocation given by Z, intentionally kills Y, Z's child. This is murder, inasmuch as the provocation was not given by the child, and the death of the child was not caused by accident or misfortune in doing an act caused by the provocation.
illustrations.key_principle: Provocation by Z cannot justify intentionally killing a third party (Y/Z's child) who did not give the provocation, except by actual accident or misfortune.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: Y gives grave and sudden provocation to A. A, on this provocation, fires a pistol at Y, neither intending nor knowing himself to be likely to kill Z, who is near him, but out of sight. A kills Z. Here A has not committed murder, but merely culpable homicide.
illustrations.key_principle: Accidental death of a bystander while acting under grave and sudden provocation reduces the offence to culpable homicide.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A is lawfully arrested by Z, a bailiff. A is excited to sudden and violent passion by the arrest, and kills Z. This is murder, inasmuch as the provocation was given by a thing done by a public servant in the exercise of his powers.
illustrations.key_principle: Proviso Secondly bars the exception — provocation arising from lawful exercise of public servant's power cannot reduce murder to culpable homicide.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A appears as a witness before Z, a Magistrate. Z says that he does not believe a word of A's deposition, and that A has perjured himself. A is moved to sudden passion by these words, and kills Z. This is murder.
illustrations.key_principle: Words alone (insults, accusations) by a public servant in lawful exercise of powers cannot constitute qualifying provocation.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A attempts to pull Z's nose. Z, in the exercise of the right of private defence, lays hold of A to prevent him from doing so. A is moved to sudden and violent passion in consequence, and kills Z. This is murder, inasmuch as the provocation was giving by a thing done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
illustrations.key_principle: Proviso Thirdly bars the exception — provocation arising from another person's lawful exercise of private defence cannot reduce murder to culpable homicide.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f)
illustrations.text: Z strikes B. B is by this provocation excited to violent rage. A, a bystander, intending to take advantage of B's rage, and to cause him to kill Z, puts a knife into B's hand for that purpose. B kills Z with the knife. Here B may have committed only culpable homicide, but A is guilty of murder.
illustrations.key_principle: A person who deliberately exploits another's provoked rage to engineer a killing cannot claim the provocation exception — they are guilty of murder.

exceptions.heading: Exceeding Right of Private Defence — Without Premeditation
exceptions.text: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender in the exercise in good faith of the right of private defence of person or property, exceeds the power given to him by law and causes the death of the person against whom he is exercising such right of defence without premeditation, and without any intention of doing more harm than is necessary for the purpose of such defence.
key_elements: Good faith exercise of right of private defence
Power is exceeded (i.e., more force than law permits)
Death results
No premeditation
No intention to do more harm than necessary

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: Z attempts to horsewhip A, not in such a manner as to cause grievous hurt to A. A draws out a pistol. Z persists in the assault. A believing in good faith that he can by no other means prevent himself from being horsewhipped, shoots Z dead. A has not committed murder, but only culpable homicide.
illustrations.key_principle: Good faith excess of private defence without premeditation reduces murder to culpable homicide, even when the force used is disproportionate to the threat.

exceptions.heading: Public Servant Acting in Good Faith Beyond Powers
exceptions.text: Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, being a public servant or aiding a public servant acting for the advancement of public justice, exceeds the powers given to him by law, and causes death by doing an act which he, in good faith, believes to be lawful and necessary for the due discharge of his duty as such public servant and without ill-will towards the person whose death is caused.
key_elements: Offender is a public servant OR aiding a public servant
Acting for advancement of public justice
Exceeds powers given by law
Genuinely believes the act to be lawful and necessary
Good faith — no ill-will towards the deceased

exceptions.heading: Sudden Fight in Heat of Passion
exceptions.text: Culpable homicide is not murder if it is committed without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel and without the offender's having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
key_elements: Sudden fight
Heat of passion
Sudden quarrel
No premeditation
No undue advantage taken
No cruel or unusual manner
exceptions.explanation: It is immaterial in such cases which party offers the provocation or commits the first assault.

exceptions.heading: Death by Consent of Person Above 18
exceptions.text: Culpable homicide is not murder when the person whose death is caused, being above the age of eighteen years, suffers death or takes the risk of death with his own consent.
key_elements: Victim is above 18 years of age
Victim consented to death or the risk of death

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, by instigation, voluntarily causes Z, a person under eighteen years of age to commit suicide. Here, on account of Z's youth, he was incapable of giving consent to his own death; A has therefore abetted murder.
illustrations.verdict: Abetted murder — exception does NOT apply
illustrations.key_principle: A person under 18 cannot give valid consent to death — the exception therefore does not apply and the instigator is liable for abetting murder.

sections.heading: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended
sections.text: If a person, by doing anything which he intends or knows to be likely to cause death, commits culpable homicide by causing the death of any person, whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause, the culpable homicide committed by the offender is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.
sections.key_principle: Doctrine of transfer of malice — the mens rea intended against the target person transfers to the unintended victim. The offence is classified as if the intended victim had died.
sections.plain_language: If A intends to kill B but accidentally kills C instead, A's liability is assessed as if C were B — the guilty intent 'transfers' to the actual victim.

sections.heading: Punishment for murder
sections.text: Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Punishment for murder by life-convict
sections.text: Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death.
key_points: Applies only where the accused is already serving a sentence of imprisonment for life at the time of committing murder.
Punishment is mandatory death — no alternative.
Note: The Supreme Court of India in Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) struck down Section 303 as unconstitutional (violative of Articles 14 and 21) — it is therefore no longer operative in practice.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder
sections.text: Whoever commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder shall be punished—

parts.condition: If the act by which death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death
punishment: Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 10 years
And shall also be liable to fine

parts.condition: If the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, or to cause such bodily injury as is likely to cause death
punishment: Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 10 years; OR

sections.key_distinction: Part I (intention) attracts the possibility of life imprisonment; Part II (knowledge only, no intention) does not — reflecting the lesser culpability of knowledge-based offences.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Causing death by negligence
sections.text: Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
key_elements: Rash OR negligent act
Act does not amount to culpable homicide
Death results from the act
sections.key_distinction: Unlike Section 299/300, Section 304A requires no intention or knowledge of likelihood of death — it covers purely accidental deaths caused by rashness or negligence (e.g., rash driving).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 27 of 1870, s. 12.

sections.heading: Dowry death

subsections.heading: Definition of dowry death
subsections.text: Where the death of a woman is caused by any burns or bodily injury or occurs otherwise than under normal circumstances within seven years of her marriage and it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or any relative of her husband for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry, such death shall be called 'dowry death', and such husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused her death.
key_elements: Death of a woman
Caused by burns, bodily injury, or otherwise than under normal circumstances
Within seven years of marriage
Soon before death, subjected to cruelty or harassment
Cruelty/harassment by husband or his relative
In connection with demand for dowry

explanation.label: Explanation
explanation.text: For the purposes of this sub-section, 'dowry' shall have the same meaning as in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (28 of 1961).

subsections.presumption: The husband or relative shall be deemed to have caused the death — this creates a statutory presumption against them.

subsections.heading: Punishment
subsections.text: Whoever commits dowry death shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life.

punishment.nature: Mandatory minimum — court cannot award less than 7 years

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 43 of 1986, s. 10 (w.e.f. 19-11-1986).

sections.heading: Abetment of suicide of child or insane person
sections.text: If any person under eighteen years of age, any insane person, any delirious person, any idiot, or any person in a state of intoxication, commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
protected_categories: Person in a state of intoxication
sections.rationale: These categories are considered incapable of giving valid consent — abetting their suicide is treated with the same severity as murder.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Abetment of suicide
sections.text: If any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_distinction_from_305: Section 306 covers abetment of suicide of a competent adult; Section 305 covers abetment involving the protected categories (minors, insane, etc.) and attracts a far harsher penalty including death.

sections.heading: Attempt to murder
sections.text: Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if hurt is caused to any person by such act, the offender shall be liable either to imprisonment for life, or to such punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned.
key_elements: Act done with intention or knowledge such that if death resulted the accused would be guilty of murder
Death need not actually result — the attempt itself is the offence

where_hurt_caused.imprisonment: Imprisonment for life OR up to 10 years of either description

sections.key_distinction: The aggravated punishment (life imprisonment) kicks in only if hurt is actually caused — making Section 307 a two-tier offence.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

chapters_covered: XVI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (sub-heading: Of Offences Affecting Life)
key_themes: Definition and degrees of culpable homicide (Section 299)
When culpable homicide escalates to murder — four clauses (Section 300)
Five exceptions reducing murder to culpable homicide (Section 300, Exceptions 1–5)
Transfer of malice doctrine (Section 301)
Punishment ladder: Murder (302) > Life-convict murder (303) > Culpable homicide (304) > Negligent death (304A)
Dowry death — special statutory offence with mandatory minimum 7 years (Section 304B)
Abetment of suicide — two tiers based on victim's capacity (Sections 305 and 306)
Attempt to murder — two-tier punishment based on whether hurt was caused (Section 307)
notable_amendments: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 — 'transportation for life' replaced by 'imprisonment for life' throughout ss. 302–307 (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Section 304A inserted by Act 27 of 1870, s. 12 — adding rash/negligent death as a distinct offence.
Section 304B inserted by Act 43 of 1986, s. 10 (w.e.f. 19-11-1986) — adding dowry death as a specific offence with a mandatory minimum sentence.
Section 303 declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) — mandatory death for life-convicts struck down under Articles 14 and 21.
metadata.case_query: A man during a sudden heated quarrel struck his neighbour repeatedly with a stick, causing his death; he claims he lost self-control after the neighbour abused him first and did not premeditate the act, while the prosecution argues the repeated blows indicate an intention to cause bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body
chapters.sub_heading: Attempts to commit offences affecting life; Thuggee

sections.heading: Attempt to commit culpable homicide
sections.text: Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and, if hurt is caused to any person by such act, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Doing an act
With intention or knowledge such that if death resulted, the accused would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder
Under circumstances where the act was capable of causing such death

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention or knowledge of the kind that would constitute culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years, or fine, or both (where no hurt is caused)
Up to seven years, or fine, or both (where hurt is caused to any person)

sections.key_principle: Mirror of Section 307 (attempt to murder) but for the lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The test is hypothetical: if death had resulted, would the accused be guilty under Section 304? Two-tier punishment — base (3 yrs) and aggravated where hurt actually results (7 yrs).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, on grave and sudden provocation, fires a pistol at Z, under such circumstances that if he thereby caused death he would be guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Grave and sudden provocation reduces the hypothetical offence from murder to culpable homicide, and so the attempt is caught by Section 308, not Section 307.

sections.heading: Attempt to commit suicide
sections.text: Whoever attempts to commit suicide and does any act towards the commission of such offence, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: An attempt to commit suicide is punishable; actual completed suicide is not (as no person survives to be prosecuted). Note: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Section 115) creates a rebuttable presumption that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress and directs the government to provide care, not prosecution — significantly limiting the practical operation of this section.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'or with fine, or with both' were substituted by Act 8 of 1882, s. 7, for 'and shall also be liable to fine'.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 8 of 1882, s. 7, for 'and shall also be liable to fine'.

sections.heading: Thug
sections.text: Whoever, at any time after the passing of this Act, shall have been habitually associated with any other or others for the purpose of committing robbery or child-stealing by means of or accompanied with murder, is a thug.
ingredients: Habitual association with one or more others
For the purpose of committing robbery or child-stealing
By means of, or accompanied with, murder
sections.key_principle: Definitional section for 'Thug' — read with Section 311 which provides punishment. A person need not have actually committed robbery or murder in a specific instance; habitual association for the purpose is sufficient.

sections.heading: Punishment (for being a Thug)
sections.text: Whoever is a thug, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Punishment provision for being a Thug as defined in Section 310. Life imprisonment is mandatory. Read together with Section 310.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body
chapters.sub_heading: Of the Causing of Miscarriage, of Injuries to Unborn Children, of the Exposure of Infants, and of the Concealment of Births

sections.heading: Causing miscarriage
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes a woman with child to miscarry, shall, if such miscarriage be not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and, if the woman be quick with child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing a woman with child to miscarry
Not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman

mens_rea_modes.description: Voluntary act — intentionally causing a pregnant woman to miscarry

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years, or fine, or both (where woman is not quick with child)
Up to seven years and also liable to fine (where woman is quick with child — i.e., foetal movement perceptible)

sections.key_principle: Two-tier punishment based on stage of pregnancy: ordinary pregnancy (up to 3 yrs) vs. quick with child — where foetal movement is perceptible (up to 7 yrs). Good-faith exception for medical necessity to save the mother's life. Note: the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 now governs lawful terminations and overrides this section for registered medical practitioners acting within its framework.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: A woman who causes herself to miscarry, is within the meaning of this section.
explanations.plain_language: A woman who self-induces a miscarriage is also liable under this section, not merely a third party who causes it.

sections.heading: Causing miscarriage without woman's consent
sections.text: Whoever commits the offence defined in the last preceding section without the consent of the woman, whether the woman is quick with child or not, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Causing a pregnant woman to miscarry (all ingredients of Section 312)
Without the consent of the woman

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Aggravated form of Section 312 — absence of the woman's consent makes this a far more serious offence (life imprisonment possible) regardless of whether the woman is quick with child or not. The stage of pregnancy is irrelevant once consent is absent.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage
sections.text: Whoever, with intent to cause the miscarriage of a woman with child, does any act which causes the death of such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if the act is done without the consent of the woman, shall be punished either with imprisonment for life, or with the punishment above mentioned.
ingredients: Intent to cause miscarriage of a pregnant woman
Doing an act in pursuance of that intent
Such act causes the death of the woman

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause miscarriage (not intent to kill — the death is an unintended consequence)

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years and also liable to fine (where act is done with woman's consent)
Or up to ten years and fine (where act is done without woman's consent)

sections.key_principle: Applies when an abortion attempt kills the mother — the intent is to miscarry, not to kill. If death results without consent, punishment escalates to life imprisonment. The Explanation clarifies that knowledge that the act is likely to cause death is not required for this offence.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: It is not essential to this offence that the offender should know that the act is likely to cause death.
explanations.plain_language: The offence is made out even if the accused did not foresee the risk of death — the intent to miscarry plus the resulting death is sufficient.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause it to die after birth
sections.text: Whoever before the birth of any child does any act with the intention of thereby preventing that child from being born alive or causing it to die after its birth, and does by such act prevent that child from being born alive, or causes it to die after its birth, shall, if such act be not caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: An act done before the birth of a child
With intention to prevent the child from being born alive OR to cause it to die after birth
The act actually achieves its intended result (child not born alive, or dies after birth)
Not done in good faith to save the life of the mother

mens_rea_modes.description: Specific intention to prevent live birth or to cause post-birth death

sections.key_principle: Distinct from Section 312 (miscarriage) — targets foeticide and infanticide where the specific intent is to prevent live birth or to kill the child after birth. Requires the act to actually achieve the lethal result. Good-faith medical exception for saving the mother applies.

sections.heading: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide
sections.text: Whoever does any act under such circumstances, that if he thereby caused death he would be guilty of culpable homicide, and does by such act cause the death of a quick unborn child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: An act done under circumstances such that if it caused human death, the accused would be guilty of culpable homicide
The act causes the death of a quick unborn child (one whose movement is perceptible)

mens_rea_modes.description: The mens rea of culpable homicide (intention to cause death / knowledge that death is likely) directed at a person, which incidentally causes the death of a quick unborn child

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Unlike Section 315, no specific intent to harm the foetus is required — the accused's culpable homicide mens rea towards any person suffices. Operates on a transferred malice-like principle: act aimed at a person (usually the pregnant woman) kills the quick unborn child instead. The child must be 'quick' (perceptible foetal movement).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, knowing that he is likely to cause the death of a pregnant woman, does an act which, if it caused the death of the woman, would amount to culpable homicide. The woman is injured, but does not die; but the death of an unborn quick child with which she is pregnant is thereby caused. A is guilty of the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.key_principle: The death of the pregnant woman is not required — injury to her combined with the resulting death of the quick unborn child is sufficient.

sections.heading: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years, by parent or person having care of it
sections.text: Whoever being the father or mother of a child under the age of twelve years, or having the care of such child, shall expose or leave such child in any place with the intention of wholly abandoning such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Being the father, mother, or person having care of a child under twelve years
Exposing or leaving the child in any place
With the intention of wholly abandoning the child

mens_rea_modes.description: Specific intention of wholly abandoning the child

sections.key_principle: Confined to persons in a position of care — parent or guardian. Intent to wholly abandon (not temporary leaving) is the mens rea. The Explanation preserves the right to also try the offender for murder or culpable homicide if the child dies as a consequence of the exposure.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: This section is not intended to prevent the trial of the offender for murder or culpable homicide, as the case may be, if the child die in consequence of the exposure.
explanations.plain_language: Section 317 and a murder/culpable homicide charge are not mutually exclusive — if the abandoned child dies, the accused can also be prosecuted under Sections 302 or 304.

sections.heading: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body
sections.text: Whoever, by secretly burying or otherwise disposing of the dead body of a child whether such child die before or after or during its birth, intentionally conceals or endeavors to conceal the birth of such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Secret burial or other disposal of the dead body of a child
Whether the child died before, after, or during birth
Intention to conceal or endeavour to conceal the birth of the child

mens_rea_modes.description: Intentional concealment of birth by secret disposal of the child's dead body

sections.key_principle: Covers stillbirths as well as neonatal deaths — the child need not have been born alive. The focus is on concealing the fact of birth, not on causing death. This section is commonly charged where the cause of the child's death is unknown or cannot be proved, as it does not require proof of the cause of death.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body

sections.heading: Hurt
sections.text: Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt.
ingredients: Causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity
To any person
sections.key_principle: Broad definitional section — any bodily pain (however minor), disease, or infirmity suffices. No minimum threshold of pain. Read with Section 321 (voluntarily causing hurt) and Section 323 (punishment). Grievous hurt is separately defined and enumerated in Section 320.

sections.heading: Grievous hurt
sections.text: The following kinds of hurt only are designated as "grievous":— First. Emasculation. Secondly. Permanent privation of the sight of either eye. Thirdly. Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear. Fourthly. Privation of any member or joint. Fifthly. Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint. Sixthly. Permanent disfiguration of the head or face. Seventhly. Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth. Eighthly. Any hurt which endangers life or which causes the sufferer to be during the space of twenty days in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits.
ingredients: One of the eight enumerated categories of hurt

grievous_hurt_categories.description: Permanent privation of the sight of either eye
Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear
Privation of any member or joint
Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint
Permanent disfiguration of the head or face
Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth
Any hurt which endangers life OR causes the sufferer during twenty days to be in severe bodily pain OR unable to follow ordinary pursuits

sections.key_principle: Exhaustive list — only these eight categories qualify as grievous hurt. The Eighth clause is the most litigated: it has three disjunctive limbs (life-endangering / 20 days severe pain / 20 days unable to follow ordinary pursuits). A simple fracture falls under the Seventh clause; whether it is permanent is irrelevant for that clause.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt
sections.text: Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does thereby cause hurt to any person, is said "voluntarily to cause hurt".
ingredients: Doing any act
With intention of causing hurt to any person; OR with knowledge that the act is likely to cause hurt to any person
The act actually causes hurt to any person (may be a different person from the one intended)

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause hurt
Knowledge that the act is likely to cause hurt

sections.key_principle: Two mens rea modes: intention (certain) and knowledge (likely). The hurt need not be caused to the intended person — transferred malice applies. Punishment is under Section 323 (simple hurt) or Section 324 (dangerous weapons/means).

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, if the hurt which he intends to cause or knows himself to be likely to cause is grievous hurt, and if the hurt which he causes is grievous hurt, is said "voluntarily to cause grievous hurt".
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt (all elements of Section 321)
The hurt intended or known to be likely is grievous hurt (Section 320)
The hurt actually caused is grievous hurt (Section 320)

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause grievous hurt
Knowledge that grievous hurt is likely to result

sections.key_principle: Requires a double coincidence: the accused must intend/know grievous hurt is likely AND grievous hurt must actually result. The Explanation clarifies that the kind of grievous hurt intended need not match the kind actually caused. Punishment under Section 325 (general) or Section 326 (dangerous weapons).

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, intending or knowing himself to be likely permanently to disfigure Z's face, gives Z a blow which does not permanently disfigure Z's face, but which causes Z to suffer severe bodily pain for the space of twenty days. A has voluntarily caused grievous hurt.
illustrations.verdict: Guilty of voluntarily causing grievous hurt
illustrations.key_principle: Though the intended kind of grievous hurt (permanent disfigurement — Sixth clause) did not occur, the actual grievous hurt (20 days severe pain — Eighth clause) still satisfies Section 322 because grievous hurt was both intended and caused, even if of a different kind.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: A person is not said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt except when he both causes grievous hurt and intends or knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt. But he is said voluntarily to cause grievous hurt, if intending or knowing himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt of one kind, he actually causes grievous hurt of another kind.
explanations.plain_language: Both the intent and the result must be grievous hurt — but they need not be grievous hurt of the same kind.

sections.heading: Punishment for voluntarily causing hurt
sections.text: Whoever, except in the case provided for by section 334, voluntarily causes hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Base punishment for voluntarily causing simple hurt. Excludes cases falling under Section 334 (provocation — lesser punishment). Cognizable but bailable.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons or means
sections.text: Whoever, except in the case provided for by section 334, voluntarily causes hurt by means of any instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, or by means of fire or any heated substance, or by means of any poison or any corrosive substance, or by means of any explosive substance or by means of any substance which it is deleterious to the human body to inhale, to swallow, or to receive into the blood, or by means of any animal, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt (Section 321)

By means of: shooting/stabbing/cutting instrument; OR any instrument likely to cause death when used as weapon; OR fire/heated substance; OR poison/corrosive substance; OR explosive substance; OR substance deleterious to the body by inhalation/swallowing/absorption into blood; OR any animal
sections.key_principle: Aggravated hurt — same act as Section 323 but committed with dangerous means. The danger lies in the means, not in the severity of the actual hurt. A common weapon like a lathi can be a 'dangerous weapon' if used in a manner likely to cause death. Excludes provocation cases (Section 334).

sections.heading: Punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt
sections.text: Whoever, except in the case provided for by section 335, voluntarily causes grievous hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Base punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt. Excludes provocation cases under Section 335. Cognizable and non-bailable.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means
sections.text: Whoever, except in the case provided for by section 335, voluntarily causes grievous hurt by means of any instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, or by means of fire or any heated substance, or by means of any poison or any corrosive substance, or by means of any explosive substance, or by means of any substance which it is deleterious to the human body to inhale, to swallow, or to receive into the blood, or by means of any animal, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt (Section 322)
By any of the dangerous means enumerated under Section 324

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Most serious hurt offence before acid attack provisions — grievous hurt by dangerous means, carrying up to life imprisonment. The combination of grievous result + dangerous means is what distinguishes this from Sections 323–325. Excludes provocation cases (Section 335).
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.
sections.text: Whoever causes permanent or partial damage or deformity to, or burns or maims or disfigures or disables, any part or parts of the body of a person or causes grievous hurt by throwing acid on or by administering acid to that person, or by using any other means with the intention of causing or with the knowledge that he is likely to cause such injury or hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine: Provided that such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses of the treatment of the victim: Provided further that any fine imposed under this section shall be paid to the victim.
ingredients: Causing permanent or partial damage/deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, or disability, or causing grievous hurt
By throwing acid on or administering acid to a person, or by any other means
With intention to cause such injury or knowledge that such injury is likely

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause the specified injury
Knowledge that the injury is likely to result

punishment_options.condition: Not less than ten years, may extend to imprisonment for life
Mandatory; must be just and reasonable to cover the victim's medical expenses; fine paid directly to the victim

sections.key_principle: Acid-attack specific provision inserted by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013. Mandatory minimum of 10 years. The fine is victim-centric — it must cover medical treatment costs and is paid directly to the victim, not the State. Partial damage is sufficient; permanence is not required (Explanation 2).
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 5 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: For the purposes of section 326A and this section, 'acid' includes any substance which has acidic or corrosive character or burning nature, that is capable of causing bodily injury leading to scars or disfigurement or temporary or permanent disability.
explanations.plain_language: Acid is broadly defined to include any corrosive or burning substance — not limited to laboratory acids.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: For the purposes of section 326A and this section, permanent or partial damage or deformity shall not be required to be irreversible.
explanations.plain_language: The damage need not be irreversible to attract this provision — partial or reversible damage still qualifies.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 5 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Voluntarily throwing or attempting to throw acid
sections.text: Whoever throws or attempts to throw acid on any person or attempts to administer acid to any person, or attempts to use any other means, with the intention of causing permanent or partial damage or deformity or burns or maiming or disfigurement or disability or grievous hurt to that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than five years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Throwing or attempting to throw acid, or attempting to administer acid, or attempting to use other means
With intention of causing permanent or partial damage, deformity, burns, maiming, disfigurement, disability, or grievous hurt

mens_rea_modes.description: Specific intention to cause any of the enumerated injuries

punishment_options.condition: Not less than five years, may extend to seven years
Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Attempt provision complementing Section 326A — covers failed acid attacks and preparatory acts. Lower mandatory minimum (5 yrs vs. 10 yrs) than the completed offence. Intent must be specifically to cause the listed injuries. The Explanations from Section 326A (definition of acid; permanence not required) apply equally here.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 5 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 5 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal act
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer, or from any person interested in the sufferer, any property or valuable security, or of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in such sufferer to do anything which is illegal or which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt

For the purpose of: extorting property or valuable security from the sufferer or persons interested; OR constraining the sufferer or persons interested to do anything illegal or to facilitate an offence

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Hurt used as a tool of extortion or coercion — purpose-driven aggravated hurt. The extortion/coercion need not succeed; causing hurt with that purpose is sufficient. Pair with Section 329 (grievous hurt for same purpose — life imprisonment possible).

sections.heading: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence
sections.text: Whoever administers to or causes to be taken by any person any poison or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug, or other thing with intent to cause hurt to such person, or with intent to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Administering to, or causing any person to take, any poison, stupefying drug, intoxicating substance, unwholesome drug, or other thing
With intent to cause hurt; OR with intent to commit or facilitate an offence; OR knowing it to be likely to cause hurt

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause hurt by the substance
Intent to commit or facilitate any offence using the substance
Knowledge that the substance is likely to cause hurt

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Covers spiking drinks or food with drugs/alcohol/poison. The offence is complete upon administration with the relevant intent — actual hurt need not result. The second mens rea mode (intent to commit any offence) makes this particularly broad — e.g., spiking a drink to facilitate robbery or sexual assault.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal act
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer any property or valuable security, or of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in such sufferer to do anything that is illegal or which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt (Section 322)
For the purpose of extorting property/valuable security or constraining to an illegal act (same purpose as Section 327)

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Aggravated version of Section 327 — same extortionate purpose but with grievous hurt instead of simple hurt, attracting life imprisonment. The Section 327/329 pair mirrors the Section 323/325 pair for base hurt/grievous hurt.
sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt, for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt

For the purpose of: extorting a confession or information leading to detection of an offence/misconduct; OR constraining restoration of property or valuable security; OR constraining satisfaction of any claim or demand; OR obtaining information leading to restoration of property

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: The primary third-degree torture provision of the IPC — expressly covers police torture to extract confessions or information (see illustrations). The illustrations explicitly name police officers and revenue officers as typical accused persons. Confession extracted under this section is inadmissible under Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act. Pair with Section 331 (grievous hurt for same purpose).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, a police-officer, tortures Z in order to induce Z to confess that he committed a crime. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Police torture to extract confession is expressly covered.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, a police-officer, tortures B to induce him to point out where certain stolen property is deposited. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Torture to obtain information about property location (not a confession) also falls within this section.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, a revenue officer, tortures Z in order to compel him to pay certain arrears of revenue due from Z. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Using hurt to compel payment of a demand (even a legitimate one) falls under the section.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A, a zamindar, tortures a raiyat in order to compel him to pay his rent. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Private persons (not just public servants) who torture to enforce payment of a claim are equally liable.

chapters_covered: XVI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body (sub-headings: Attempts to commit offences affecting life / Thuggee; Of the Causing of Miscarriage...; Of Hurt)
key_themes: Attempt to commit culpable homicide — two-tier punishment based on whether hurt is caused (Section 308)
Attempt to commit suicide — simple imprisonment up to 1 year; limited in practice by MHA 2017 (Section 309)
Thuggee — definition and mandatory life imprisonment (Sections 310–311)
Causing miscarriage — two-tier by stage of pregnancy; aggravated without consent (Sections 312–313)
Death from miscarriage attempt — no knowledge of death required; escalates to life if without consent (Section 314)
Foeticide and infanticide — intent to prevent live birth or cause post-birth death (Section 315)
Death of quick unborn child by culpable homicide act — transferred malice to foetus (Section 316)
Child abandonment — parent/guardian; wholly abandoning under-12; Section 302/304 trial preserved (Section 317)
Concealment of birth by secret disposal — covers stillbirths; no proof of cause of death needed (Section 318)
Hurt and grievous hurt — definitional sections (Sections 319–322); exhaustive 8-category grievous hurt list (Section 320)
Voluntarily causing hurt — base (1 yr) and dangerous weapons (3 yrs) (Sections 323–324)
Voluntarily causing grievous hurt — base (7 yrs) and dangerous weapons (life) (Sections 325–326)
Acid attack — mandatory minimum 10 yrs / attempt 5 yrs; fine paid to victim (Sections 326A–326B, inserted 2013)
Extortionate hurt — purpose of extorting property/constraining illegal act: simple hurt (10 yrs) / grievous hurt (life) (Sections 327, 329)
Poison/drug administration — covers drink-spiking; intent to commit any offence (Section 328)
Torture to extract confession / compel restoration — anti-third-degree provision; police expressly illustrated (Section 330)
notable_amendments: Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 — 'transportation for life' replaced by 'imprisonment for life' in Sections 311, 313, 326, 329 (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Act 8 of 1882, s. 7 — Section 309 punishment amended to add 'or with fine, or with both'.
Act 13 of 2013, s. 5 — Sections 326A and 326B inserted (acid attacks) with mandatory minimums (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).
Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s. 115 — creates rebuttable presumption of severe stress for suicide attempt; directs care not prosecution, significantly curtailing Section 309.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from any person interested in the sufferer any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security, or to satisfy any claim or demand or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt (Section 322)

For the purpose of: extorting a confession or information leading to detection of an offence/misconduct; OR constraining restoration of property or valuable security; OR satisfying any claim or demand; OR obtaining information leading to restoration of property

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Aggravated version of Section 330 — identical purpose (extorting confession / compelling restoration) but with grievous hurt instead of simple hurt, doubling the maximum punishment from 7 to 10 years. The Section 330/331 pair for confessions mirrors the Section 327/329 pair for extorting property.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt to deter public servant from his duty
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt to any person being a public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person or any other public servant from discharging his duty as such public servant or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by that person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt

To a person who is a public servant in the discharge of duty; OR with intent to prevent/deter that or any other public servant from discharging duty; OR in consequence of anything done/attempted in lawful discharge of duty

mens_rea_modes.description: Voluntary causing of hurt with the specified public-servant nexus — includes retaliatory hurt for past lawful acts

sections.key_principle: Three triggers: (1) hurt during duty discharge, (2) intent to prevent/deter any public servant, (3) retaliation for past lawful acts. Covers attacks on police, revenue officers, and any public servant acting within their authority. Pair with Section 333 (grievous hurt — same triggers, up to 10 years).

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt to any person being a public servant in the discharge of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person or any other public servant from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by that person in the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt (Section 322)
Same three-limb public servant nexus as Section 332

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Aggravated version of Section 332 — grievous hurt to a public servant in the same three scenarios, maximum raised from 3 to 10 years. Non-bailable and cognizable.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt on provocation
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing hurt
On grave and sudden provocation
The accused neither intends nor knows himself likely to cause hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation

mens_rea_modes.description: Hurt caused in the heat of grave and sudden provocation, directed only at the provoker

sections.key_principle: Provocation exception for simple hurt — the offence is carved out of Section 323. The same provisos as Exception 1 to Section 300 apply (Explanation under Section 335): provocation must not be self-sought, must not arise from lawful acts of a public servant, and must not arise from the exercise of the right of private defence.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt on provocation
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to four years, or with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt
On grave and sudden provocation
The accused neither intends nor knows himself likely to cause grievous hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation
sections.key_principle: Provocation exception for grievous hurt — carved out of Section 325. Both Sections 334 and 335 are subject to the same provisos as Exception 1 to Section 300 (Explanation appended after Section 335).

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: The last two sections are subject to the same provisos as Exception 1, section 300.
explanations.plain_language: Sections 334 and 335 both require that: (a) the provocation was not sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse; (b) the provocation did not arise from anything done in obedience to law or by a public servant in lawful exercise of powers; and (c) the provocation did not arise from the exercise of the right of private defence.

sections.amendment_note: The word 'voluntarily' was inserted by Act 8 of 1882, s. 8.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 8 of 1882, s. 8.

sections.heading: Act endangering life or personal safety of others
sections.text: Whoever does any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months or with fine which may extend to two hundred and fifty rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Doing any act
So rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others

mens_rea_modes.description: Rashness — doing an act with consciousness of risk but without caring about it
Negligence — doing an act without consciousness of the risk that a reasonable person would have foreseen

punishment_options.condition: Up to two hundred and fifty rupees

sections.key_principle: Base offence for rash/negligent endangerment — no actual hurt required, endangerment is sufficient. Read as a ladder with Sections 337 and 338: Section 336 (endangerment alone), Section 337 (hurt results), Section 338 (grievous hurt results). Commonly invoked in traffic and workplace accidents.

sections.heading: Causing hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others
sections.text: Whoever causes hurt to any person by doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Causing hurt to any person
By doing an act rashly or negligently
Such that the act endangered human life or the personal safety of others
sections.key_principle: Mid-tier of the rash/negligent ladder — hurt actually results. Standard charge in road accident cases where the victim survives with simple injuries. Compare with Section 304A (rash/negligent act causing death) for fatal accidents.

sections.heading: Causing grievous hurt by act endangering life or personal safety of others
sections.text: Whoever causes grievous hurt to any person by doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Causing grievous hurt (Section 320) to any person
By doing an act rashly or negligently
Such that the act endangered human life or the personal safety of others
sections.key_principle: Top of the rash/negligent ladder for non-fatal outcomes — grievous hurt results. Common charge in serious road accidents, industrial accidents, and medical negligence cases where the victim suffers grievous injuries but survives. Bailable.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body
chapters.sub_heading: Of Wrongful Restraint and Wrongful Confinement

sections.heading: Wrongful restraint
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person.
ingredients: Voluntary obstruction of a person
So as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction
In which that person has a right to proceed
sections.key_principle: Definitional section — read with Section 341 (punishment). Partial restraint suffices; it need not be total confinement within limits (that is Section 340). The Exception carves out good-faith obstruction of a private way the person believes he has a lawful right to block.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A obstructs a path along which Z has a right to pass, A not believing in good faith that he has a right to stop the path. Z is thereby prevented from passing. A wrongfully restrains Z.
illustrations.key_principle: The absence of good faith in believing the right to obstruct is decisive.

exceptions.label: Exception
exceptions.text: The obstruction of a private way over land or water which a person in good faith believes himself to have a lawful right to obstruct, is not an offence within the meaning of this section.
exceptions.plain_language: Obstructing a private path that the accused genuinely and in good faith believes he is entitled to block is not wrongful restraint.

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said "wrongfully to confine" that person.
ingredients: Wrongful restraint (Section 339)
Such that the person is prevented from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits in every direction
sections.key_principle: Wrongful confinement is a species of wrongful restraint — every confinement involves restraint, but not every restraint is confinement. Confinement requires the person to be hemmed in on all sides within circumscribing limits. Read with Section 342 (punishment) and Sections 343–348 (aggravated forms).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A causes Z to go within a walled space, and locks Z in. Z is thus prevented from proceeding in any direction beyond the circumscribing line of wall. A wrongfully confines Z.
illustrations.key_principle: Physical enclosure within walls from which there is no exit constitutes wrongful confinement.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A places men with firearms at the outlets of a building, and tells Z that they will fire at Z if Z attempts to leave the building. A wrongfully confines Z.
illustrations.key_principle: Confinement by threat of force at every exit is as effective as physical lock-and-key — the means of confinement need not be physical barriers.

sections.heading: Punishment for wrongful restraint
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully restrains any person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Punishment for base wrongful restraint (Section 339). Note simple imprisonment only — not rigorous. Bailable and compoundable.

sections.heading: Punishment for wrongful confinement
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Base punishment for wrongful confinement (Section 340). Sections 343–348 provide aggravated punishments based on duration, secrecy, or purpose of confinement.

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement for three or more days
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person for three days, or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Wrongful confinement (Section 340)
For three or more days
sections.key_principle: First duration-based aggravation of wrongful confinement — three days triggers a doubling of the maximum from 1 year to 2 years. Pair with Section 344 (ten or more days — 3 years).

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement for ten or more days
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person for ten days, or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Wrongful confinement (Section 340)
For ten or more days

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Second duration-based aggravation — ten days raises the maximum to 3 years and makes fine mandatory (in addition to imprisonment). The mandatory fine structure mirrors that of the more serious hurt offences.

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement of person for whose liberation writ has been issued
sections.text: Whoever keeps any person in wrongful confinement, knowing that a writ for the liberation of that person has been duly issued, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years in addition to any term of imprisonment to which he may be liable under any other section of this Chapter.
ingredients: Keeping any person in wrongful confinement
Knowing that a writ for the liberation of that person has been duly issued

mens_rea_modes.description: Knowledge that a writ of liberation (e.g. habeas corpus) has been duly issued

punishment_options.condition: Up to two years — in ADDITION to any punishment under any other section of this Chapter

sections.key_principle: Designed to enforce compliance with court orders — defying a habeas corpus or similar writ by continuing confinement attracts an additional consecutive punishment on top of the base wrongful confinement sentence. Knowledge of the writ is an essential ingredient.

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement in secret
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person in such manner as to indicate an intention that the confinement of such person may not be known to any person interested in the person so confined, or to any public servant, or that the place of such confinement may not be known to or discovered by any such person or public servant as hereinbefore mentioned, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years in addition to any other punishment to which he may be liable for such wrongful confinement.
ingredients: Wrongful confinement

In a manner indicating intention that: the fact of confinement shall not be known to persons interested in the confined person or to any public servant; OR the place of confinement shall not be discoverable by such persons or public servants

punishment_options.condition: Up to two years — in ADDITION to any other punishment for the wrongful confinement itself

sections.key_principle: Secrecy-based aggravation — the additional punishment recognises that secret confinement denies the confined person access to legal remedies (habeas corpus, police complaint) and is therefore more culpable. The additional 2 years stacks on top of the base confinement punishment and any other applicable sections.

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement to extort property, or constrain to illegal act
sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined, or from any person interested in the person confined, any property or valuable security or of constraining the person confined or any person interested in such person to do anything illegal or to give any information which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Wrongful confinement

For the purpose of: extorting property or valuable security from the confined person or persons interested; OR constraining the confined person or persons interested to do anything illegal; OR constraining them to give information facilitating commission of an offence

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Confinement used as a coercive tool for extortion or illegal coercion — purpose-based aggravation of wrongful confinement. The confinement is the means, not an end in itself. Contrast with Section 348 (confinement to extract confession/information about a past offence).

sections.heading: Wrongful confinement to extort confession, or compel restoration of property
