sections.text: Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined or any person interested in the person confined any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the person confined or any person interested in the person confined to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Wrongful confinement

For the purpose of: extorting a confession or information leading to detection of an offence/misconduct; OR constraining restoration of property or valuable security; OR satisfying any claim or demand; OR obtaining information leading to restoration of property

punishment_options.condition: Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Confinement-based parallel to Sections 330/331 (hurt to extract confession). Covers illegal lock-up of suspects to coerce confessions. The three-year maximum is the same as Section 347, but the purpose here is backward-looking (past offence detection / property restoration) rather than forward-looking (facilitating a future offence).

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body

sections.heading: Force
sections.text: A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other's body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling: Provided that the person causing the motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion, causes that motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion in one of the three ways hereinafter described: First. By his own bodily power. Secondly. By disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion or change or cessation of motion takes place without any further act on his part, or on the part of any other person. Thirdly. By inducing any animal to move, to change its motion, or to cease to move.
ingredients: Causing motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to another person; OR causing a substance to move so as to contact any part of another's body, clothing, or carried items, or anything affecting that person's sense of feeling
By one of three means: own bodily power; disposing a substance so that motion results without further act; inducing an animal to move

force_modes.description: By his own bodily power (e.g. pushing, striking)
By disposing any substance such that motion/change/cessation results without further act (e.g. unfastening a boat's moorings, releasing a boulder)
By inducing any animal to move, change motion, or cease to move (e.g. setting a dog on someone)

sections.key_principle: Broad definition of 'force' — encompasses indirect acts and acts through animals/substances. Mere force is not an offence; it becomes criminal force under Section 350 when done intentionally without consent for a prohibited purpose. Foundational definition for the entire assault and criminal force cluster (Sections 349–358).

sections.heading: Criminal force
sections.text: Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other.
ingredients: Intentional use of force (Section 349) to any person
Without that person's consent
In order to commit any offence; OR intending to cause injury, fear, or annoyance; OR knowing it is likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance

mens_rea_modes.description: Force used to commit any offence
Force intended to cause injury, fear, or annoyance
Force known to be likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance

sections.key_principle: Three disjunctive limbs make this very broad — the third limb (knowledge of likely annoyance) makes even minor intentional contact without consent potentially criminal force. Punishment under Sections 352–358 depending on circumstances. Distinct from assault (Section 351) which requires no actual force — only apprehension of imminent force.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: Z is sitting in a moored boat on a river. A unfastens the moorings, and thus intentionally causes the boat to drift down the stream. A has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done so without Z's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending or knowing it to be likely that this use of force will cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, A has used criminal force to Z.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — indirect act through disposing a substance
illustrations.key_principle: Force through indirect means (unfastening moorings) qualifies — no direct physical contact needed.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: Z is riding in a chariot. A lashes Z's horses, and thereby causes them to quicken their pace. A has caused change of motion to Z by inducing the animals to change their motion. A has therefore used force to Z.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — force through inducing animals
illustrations.key_principle: Causing an animal to produce motion in another person constitutes force under the third mode of Section 349.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: Z is riding in a palanquin. A, intending to rob Z, seizes the pole and stops the palanquin. A has caused cessation of motion to Z by his own bodily power. A has used criminal force to Z.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — cessation of motion to rob
illustrations.key_principle: Stopping another's movement (cessation of motion) by bodily power in order to commit an offence is criminal force.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A intentionally pushes against Z in the street without Z's consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy Z. He has used criminal force to Z.
illustrations.key_principle: An intentional push without consent intending annoyance is criminal force even without injury.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A throws a stone intending or knowing it to be likely that the stone will be brought into contact with Z or Z's clothes. If the stone produces that effect, A has used force to Z, and if done without Z's consent intending to injure, frighten or annoy, he has used criminal force.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — substance brought into contact via throwing
illustrations.key_principle: Causing a substance to contact another's body or clothing is force under Section 349; if done without consent with the requisite intent it is criminal force.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f)
illustrations.text: A intentionally pulls up a woman's veil without her consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy her. He has used criminal force to her.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — contact with clothing/item worn
illustrations.key_principle: Contact with clothing or items worn by a person constitutes force within Section 349.

illustrations.label: Illustration (g)
illustrations.text: Z is bathing. A pours boiling water into the bath. A has caused motion in the boiling water bringing it into contact with Z, and if done without Z's consent intending to cause injury, fear or annoyance, A has used criminal force.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — substance caused to contact body
illustrations.key_principle: Causing a dangerous substance to flow into contact with another's body is criminal force.

illustrations.label: Illustration (h)
illustrations.text: A incites a dog to spring upon Z, without Z's consent. Here, if A intends to cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, he uses criminal force to Z.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal force — force through inducing an animal
illustrations.key_principle: Inciting an animal to attack or touch another person constitutes force under the third mode of Section 349.

sections.heading: Assault
sections.text: Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault.
ingredients: Making any gesture or any preparation
Intending, or knowing it to be likely, that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that the maker is about to use criminal force to that person

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent that the gesture/preparation will cause apprehension of imminent criminal force
Knowledge that the gesture/preparation is likely to cause such apprehension

sections.key_principle: Assault under IPC is exclusively apprehension-based — no physical contact or force is required. It is the anticipation of imminent criminal force, not its execution. Mere words cannot amount to assault (Explanation), but words can give meaning to a gesture that makes it an assault (Illustration c). Punishment under Section 352 (general) and Sections 353–358 (aggravated circumstances).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A shakes his fist at Z, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that A is about to strike Z. A has committed an assault.
illustrations.key_principle: A threatening gesture causing apprehension of imminent strike is assault even without any contact.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A begins to unloose the muzzle of a ferocious dog, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that he is about to cause the dog to attack Z. A has committed an assault upon Z.
illustrations.key_principle: A preparatory act (unloosing a dog's muzzle) causing apprehension is an assault — no words or direct gesture needed.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A takes up a stick, saying to Z, 'I will give you a beating'. Though the words alone cannot amount to an assault, and the gesture alone might not, the gesture explained by the words may amount to an assault.
illustrations.verdict: Assault — words give meaning to the gesture
illustrations.key_principle: Words alone are not assault, but words can elevate an ambiguous gesture to an assault by clarifying threatening intent.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: Mere words do not amount to an assault. But the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparation such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault.
explanations.plain_language: No verbal threat, however serious, is an assault by itself. But accompanying words can make an otherwise ambiguous gesture amount to assault by clarifying the threatening intent.

sections.heading: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Assault (Section 351) or criminal force (Section 350)
Otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person
sections.key_principle: Base punishment for assault/criminal force. The Explanation identifies three situations where grave and sudden provocation will NOT mitigate: (1) provocation sought by the offender as an excuse, (2) provocation arising from a public servant's lawful acts, (3) provocation arising from the exercise of the right of private defence. The mitigated provocation offence is under Section 358.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: Grave and sudden provocation will not mitigate the punishment for an offence under this section, if the provocation is sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for the offence, or if the provocation is given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant, in the lawful exercise of the powers of such public servant, or if the provocation is given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence. Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to mitigate the offence, is a question of fact.
explanations.plain_language: Three situations where provocation is no mitigation: self-induced provocation, provocation from lawful state action, and provocation from lawful self-defence. Whether provocation was grave and sudden is always a question of fact.

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person being a public servant in the execution of his duty as such public servant, or with intent to prevent or deter that person from discharging his duty as such public servant, or in consequence of anything done or attempted to be done by such person to the lawful discharge of his duty as such public servant, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force
To a public servant in execution of duty; OR with intent to prevent/deter that public servant from duty; OR in consequence of the public servant's lawful acts
sections.key_principle: Assault/criminal force equivalent of Section 332 (hurt to deter public servant) — but note Section 353 carries only 2 years whereas Section 332 carries 3 years, because Section 353 requires no actual hurt. Covers police officers, revenue officials, and any public servant in execution of lawful duty.

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, intending to outrage or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Assault (Section 351) or criminal force (Section 350)
Against any woman
With intent to outrage her modesty; OR knowing it to be likely to outrage her modesty

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to outrage modesty
Knowledge that modesty is likely to be outraged

punishment_options.condition: Not less than one year, may extend to five years
Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Mandatory minimum of one year introduced by Act 13 of 2013. 'Modesty' is not defined in the IPC; the Supreme Court has held it is an attribute associated with female human beings as a class. The test is objective — whether a reasonable person would view the act as one which could outrage the modesty of a woman. Supplemented by Sections 354A–354D inserted in 2013.
sections.amendment_note: Punishment substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 6 — earlier the maximum was 2 years without a mandatory minimum (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 6, for 'shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both' (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Sexual harassment and punishment for sexual harassment
sections.text: A man committing any of the following acts — (i) physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures; or (ii) a demand or request for sexual favours; or (iii) showing pornography against the will of a woman; or (iv) making sexually coloured remarks, shall be guilty of the offence of sexual harassment. Any man who commits the offence specified in clause (i) or clause (ii) or clause (iii) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Any man who commits the offence specified in clause (iv) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: By a man

Any of four acts: (i) unwelcome physical contact/advances with explicit sexual overtures; (ii) demand/request for sexual favours; (iii) showing pornography against will of woman; (iv) making sexually coloured remarks

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years, or fine, or both — for clauses (i), (ii), and (iii)
Up to one year, or fine, or both — for clause (iv) (sexually coloured remarks)

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013 to give statutory teeth to the Vishakha guidelines on sexual harassment at workplace. Two-tier punishment — physical/coercive conduct (clauses i–iii) attracts rigorous imprisonment up to 3 years; verbal harassment (clause iv) up to 1 year. Offence is gender-specific — perpetrator must be a man, victim a woman.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe
sections.text: Any man who assaults or uses criminal force to any woman or abets such act with the intention of disrobing or compelling her to be naked, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force to a woman, or abetment of such act
With intention of disrobing her or compelling her to be naked

punishment_options.condition: Not less than three years, may extend to seven years
Also liable in addition to imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013 — specifically targets forcible disrobing and non-consensual nudity. Abetment is expressly included. Mandatory minimum of 3 years. A more specific and serious provision than Section 354 (outraging modesty) when disrobing is the specific intent.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Voyeurism
sections.text: Any man who watches, or captures the image of a woman engaging in a private act in circumstances where she would usually have the expectation of not being observed either by the perpetrator or by any other person at the behest of the perpetrator or disseminates such image shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than one year, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine, and be punished on a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Watching OR capturing the image of a woman in a private act where she expects not to be observed; OR disseminating such image
By a man

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of either description (mandatory minimum — first conviction)
punishment_options.condition: Not less than one year, may extend to three years; also liable to fine

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of either description (mandatory minimum — second/subsequent conviction)
punishment_options.condition: Not less than three years, may extend to seven years; also liable to fine

sections.key_principle: Escalating punishment on repeat conviction. 'Private act' is broadly defined (Explanation 1) to include exposure of genitals, posterior or breasts; use of lavatory; sexual acts not ordinarily done in public. Importantly, Explanation 2 covers non-consensual dissemination — even if the woman consented to being filmed, sharing without consent is an offence under this section.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: For the purpose of this section, 'private act' includes an act of watching carried out in a place which, in the circumstances, would reasonably be expected to provide privacy and where the victim's genitals, posterior or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear; or the victim is using a lavatory; or the victim is doing a sexual act that is not of a kind ordinarily done in public.
explanations.plain_language: A 'private act' covers any situation where the woman's intimate body parts are exposed or she is in a lavatory or engaged in sexual activity in a context where privacy would reasonably be expected.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Where the victim consents to the capture of the images or any act, but not to their dissemination to third persons and where such image or act is disseminated, such dissemination shall be considered an offence under this section.
explanations.plain_language: Consent to filming does not imply consent to sharing. Non-consensual distribution (revenge pornography) is independently an offence even if filming was consensual.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Stalking
sections.text: Any man who — (i) follows a woman and contacts, or attempts to contact such woman to foster personal interaction repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest by such woman; or (ii) monitors the use by a woman of the internet, email or any other form of electronic communication, commits the offence of stalking. Whoever commits the offence of stalking shall be punished on first conviction with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine; and be punished on a second or subsequent conviction, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: By a man
Following a woman and contacting or attempting to contact her repeatedly to foster personal interaction despite her clear disinterest; OR monitoring her internet/email/electronic communications

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years; also liable to fine
Up to five years; also liable to fine

sections.key_principle: Two-limb definition: physical following/contact and cyber-monitoring. Three defences available to the accused — law-enforcement purpose, compliance with a legal condition, or reasonableness and justification in the circumstances. Escalating punishment on repeat conviction. The 'clear indication of disinterest' element makes this a conduct-plus-response offence.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

exceptions.label: Proviso (defences)
exceptions.text: Such conduct shall not amount to stalking if the man proves: (i) it was pursued for preventing/detecting crime and he was entrusted with that responsibility by the State; or (ii) it was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by law; or (iii) in the particular circumstances such conduct was reasonable and justified.
exceptions.plain_language: Three defences: state-authorised surveillance, legal compliance, and reasonable justification — each is an affirmative defence the accused must prove.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 7 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force
Specifically intending to dishonour that person
Otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person
sections.key_principle: Purpose-specific assault — the intent to dishonour (e.g., shoe-beating, spitting, stripping in public) elevates the offence beyond the base Section 352 (3 months) to 2 years. The intent to dishonour is the essential ingredient distinguishing this from Section 352.

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting to commit theft on any property which that person is then wearing or carrying, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force
In attempting to commit theft
On property which that person is then wearing or carrying
sections.key_principle: Targets snatch-and-grab theft involving assault or criminal force — bag-snatching, chain-snatching. The theft need only be attempted; it need not succeed. Property must be on the person (worn or carried) at the time of the assault.

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force in attempt wrongfully to confine a person
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, in attempting wrongfully to confine that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force
In attempting wrongfully to confine that person (Section 340)
sections.key_principle: Covers forcible abduction attempts where the accused physically assaults the victim in the process of trying to confine them. The confinement need only be attempted. Distinct from kidnapping (which involves taking away or enticement) — this section is purely about the force used in an attempted confinement.

sections.heading: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation
sections.text: Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Assault or criminal force
On grave and sudden provocation given by that person
sections.key_principle: Provocation mitigant for assault/criminal force — the Section 352/358 pair mirrors the Section 323/334 pair for hurt. Same Explanation as Section 352 applies (the Explanation to Section 358 cross-references it). Only simple imprisonment, not rigorous. The fine ceiling (Rs 200) is significantly lower than Section 352 (Rs 500).

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: The last section is subject to the same Explanation as section 352.
explanations.plain_language: The same three situations where provocation does not mitigate under Section 352 apply equally here: self-induced provocation, provocation from lawful public servant acts, and provocation from lawful exercise of private defence.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Affecting the Human Body
chapters.sub_heading: Of Kidnapping, Abduction, Slavery and Forced Labour

sections.heading: Kidnapping
sections.text: Kidnapping is of two kinds: kidnapping from India, and kidnapping from lawful guardianship.
sections.key_principle: Classification section — identifies the two distinct species of kidnapping defined in Sections 360 and 361 respectively. The two kinds are mutually exclusive in their elements and can be charged together or alternatively.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.

sections.heading: Kidnapping from India
sections.text: Whoever conveys any person beyond the limits of India without the consent of that person, or of some person legally authorised to consent on behalf of that person, is said to kidnap that person from India.
ingredients: Conveying any person beyond the limits of India
Without the consent of that person; OR without the consent of a person legally authorised to consent on their behalf
sections.key_principle: No age restriction — applies to any person regardless of age, unlike Section 361 (guardianship kidnapping) which is confined to minors and persons of unsound mind. The act is crossing India's territorial limits without consent. Consent of the person or their legal representative is a complete defence. Punishment under Section 363.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.

sections.heading: Kidnapping from lawful guardianship
sections.text: Whoever takes or entices any minor under sixteen years of age if a male, or under eighteen years of age if a female, or any person of unsound mind, out of the keeping of the lawful guardian of such minor or person of unsound mind, without the consent of such guardian, is said to kidnap such minor or person from lawful guardianship.
ingredients: Takes or entices a minor (male under 16, female under 18) OR any person of unsound mind
Out of the keeping of the lawful guardian
Without the consent of such guardian
sections.key_principle: Protects the guardian's right of custody, not the minor's freedom. Consent of the minor is irrelevant — only the guardian's consent matters. 'Takes' implies physical removal; 'entices' covers inducement, persuasion, or lure. Exception: a father acting in good faith regarding an illegitimate child, or anyone acting in good faith believing they have lawful custody, is exempt unless acting for an immoral or unlawful purpose. Punishment under Section 363.

explanations.explanation_text: The words 'lawful guardian' in this section include any person lawfully entrusted with the care or custody of such minor or other person.

exceptions: This section does not extend to the act of any person who in good faith believes himself to be the father of an illegitimate child, or who in good faith believes himself to be entitled to the lawful custody of such child, unless such act is committed for an immoral or unlawful purpose.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.
Substituted by Act 42 of 1949, s. 2, for 'fourteen'.
Substituted by s. 2, ibid., for 'sixteen'.

sections.heading: Abduction
sections.text: Whoever by force compels, or by any deceitful means induces, any person to go from any place, is said to abduct that person.
ingredients: By force compels OR by deceitful means induces
Any person (no age restriction)
To go from any place
sections.key_principle: Abduction differs from kidnapping in two key ways: (1) it applies to any person regardless of age — no minor/unsound-mind restriction; (2) it is not an offence by itself but is an ingredient of several aggravated offences (Sections 364–369). It is a continuing act — repeated use of force or deceit to keep the person moving constitutes abduction at each stage. Consent obtained by deceit is no consent.

sections.heading: Punishment for kidnapping
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps any person from India or from lawful guardianship, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnapping from India (Section 360) OR from lawful guardianship (Section 361)
sections.key_principle: Base punishment provision for both species of kidnapping. Fine is mandatory (not alternative). Cognizable and non-bailable offence. Where kidnapping is accompanied by an aggravated purpose (murder, ransom, grievous hurt, etc.), Sections 363A–369 or 364A apply instead with heavier punishment.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.

sections.heading: Kidnapping or maiming a minor for purposes of begging
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps any minor or, not being the lawful guardian of a minor, obtains the custody of the minor, in order that such minor may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Whoever maims any minor in order that such minor may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Where any person, not being the lawful guardian of a minor, employs or uses such minor for the purposes of begging, it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that he kidnapped or otherwise obtained the custody of that minor in order that the minor might be employed or used for the purposes of begging.
ingredients: Kidnaps a minor OR (not being lawful guardian) obtains custody of a minor
With intent to employ/use the minor for begging — punishable up to 10 years imprisonment + fine
OR: maims any minor for purpose of begging — punishable with imprisonment for life + fine

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine — for kidnapping/obtaining custody for begging
Plus fine — for maiming a minor for begging

sections.key_principle: Addresses exploitation of minors through organised begging rackets. Sub-section (3) creates a statutory presumption — a non-guardian found employing a minor for begging is presumed to have kidnapped or unlawfully obtained custody; the burden shifts to the accused to rebut. 'Begging' defined in sub-section (4) to include soliciting alms, entering premises for alms, exhibiting deformity/disease for alms, and using a minor as exhibit.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 52 of 1959, s. 2 (w.e.f. 15-1-1960).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 52 of 1959, s. 2 (w.e.f. 15-1-1960).

sections.heading: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person in order that such person may be murdered or may be so disposed of as to be put in danger of being murdered, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnapping (Section 360/361) OR abduction (Section 362)
In order that the person may be murdered OR disposed of so as to be put in danger of being murdered

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: The purpose of murder need not be achieved — the intent at the time of kidnapping/abduction is sufficient. 'Disposed of as to be put in danger of being murdered' extends the section to cases where the kidnapper hands the victim to another with lethal intent.
illustrations: A kidnaps Z from India, intending or knowing it to be likely that Z may be sacrificed to an idol. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
A forcibly carries or entices B away from his home in order that B may be murdered. A has committed the offence defined in this section.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.
Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Kidnapping for ransom, etc.
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person or keeps a person in detention after such kidnapping or abduction, and threatens to cause death or hurt to such person, or by his conduct gives rise to a reasonable apprehension that such person may be put to death or hurt, or causes hurt or death to such person in order to compel the Government or any foreign State or international inter-governmental organisation or any other person to do or abstain from doing any act or to pay a ransom, shall be punishable with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnaps or abducts any person OR keeps a person in detention after kidnapping/abduction
Threatens death or hurt OR conduct giving reasonable apprehension of death or hurt, OR actually causes hurt or death
In order to compel Government/foreign State/international organisation/any person to do/abstain from doing any act OR to pay ransom
sections.key_principle: Inserted in 1993 to address the surge in kidnapping for ransom. The offence is complete when the threat is communicated; actual payment of ransom or harm to victim is not required. 'Any other person' extended the scope beyond state-directed demands to private ransom. Fine is mandatory in addition to death or life imprisonment.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 42 of 1993, s. 2. 'Any foreign State or international inter-governmental organisation or any other person' substituted for 'any other person' by Act 24 of 1995, s. 2.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 42 of 1993, s. 2.
Substituted by Act 24 of 1995, s. 2, for 'any other person'.

sections.heading: Kidnapping or abducting with intent secretly and wrongfully to confine person
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person with intent to cause that person to be secretly and wrongfully confined, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnaps (Section 360/361) OR abducts (Section 362) any person
With intent to cause that person to be secretly and wrongfully confined

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: The twin qualifiers 'secretly' and 'wrongfully' must both be present. Secret confinement implies concealment from those who might rescue the victim. Wrongful confinement is defined in Section 340. Intent at the time of kidnapping/abduction is the gist of the offence; actual confinement need not be established.

sections.heading: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc.
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any woman with intent that she may be compelled, or knowing it to be likely that she will be compelled, to marry any person against her will, or in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, or knowing it to be likely that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and whoever, by means of criminal intimidation as defined in this Code or of abuse of authority or any other method of compulsion, induces any woman to go from any place with intent that she may be, or knowing that it is likely that she will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person shall also be punishable as aforesaid.
ingredients: Kidnaps or abducts any woman
With intent/knowledge that she will be compelled to marry against her will, OR forced/seduced to illicit intercourse
OR: by criminal intimidation, abuse of authority, or compulsion induces any woman to go from any place with same intent/knowledge

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Gender-specific provision protecting women from forced marriage and sexual exploitation through kidnapping. Extended by Act 20 of 1923 to cover inducement through criminal intimidation or abuse of authority — covering cases where physical kidnapping is absent but coercion achieves the same result. Illicit intercourse means intercourse outside a legally recognised union.
sections.amendment_note: Extended by Act 20 of 1923, s. 2 to include inducement through criminal intimidation or abuse of authority.

footnotes.note_text: Added by Act 20 of 1923, s. 2.

sections.heading: Procuration of minor girl
sections.text: Whoever, by any means whatsoever, induces any minor girl under the age of eighteen years to go from any place or to do any act with intent that such girl may be, or knowing that it is likely that she will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: By any means whatsoever
Induces a minor girl under 18 years to go from any place OR to do any act
With intent/knowledge that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 20 of 1923. Wider than Section 366 in means — 'by any means whatsoever' covers online grooming, social media enticement, etc. Narrower than 366 in victim — confined to minor girls under 18. The phrase 'to do any act' extends beyond physical movement to any act that facilitates the illicit intercourse.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 20 of 1923, s. 3.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 20 of 1923, s. 3.

sections.heading: Importation of girl from foreign country
sections.text: Whoever imports into India from any country outside India any girl under the age of twenty-one years with intent that she may be, or knowing it to be likely that she will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Imports into India from any country outside India
Any girl under 21 years of age
With intent/knowledge that she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Cross-border trafficking provision. Age threshold (21) is higher than Sections 366A (18) or Section 361 (16/18), reflecting the vulnerability of young women imported from abroad. The words 'or from the State of Jammu and Kashmir' were inserted by Act 3 of 1951 and subsequently removed.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 20 of 1923, s. 3. Words 'or from the State of Jammu and Kashmir' inserted by Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch. The words 'British India' have successively been substituted to read 'India'.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.

sections.heading: Kidnapping or abducting in order to subject person to grievous hurt, slavery, etc.
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any person in order that such person may be subjected, or may be so disposed of as to be put in danger of being subjected to grievous hurt, or slavery, or to the unnatural lust of any person, or knowing it to be likely that such person will be so subjected or disposed of, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnaps or abducts any person
In order to subject the person (or put them in danger of being subjected) to: grievous hurt, OR slavery, OR unnatural lust of any person

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Umbrella provision covering grievous hurt, slavery, and unnatural offences as the purpose behind kidnapping/abduction. Knowledge of likelihood (as alternative to intent) broadens criminal liability — the offender need not positively intend the harm; awareness that it is likely suffices. 'Unnatural lust' covers offences under Section 377.

sections.heading: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person
sections.text: Whoever, knowing that any person has been kidnapped or has been abducted, wrongfully conceals or confines such person, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had kidnapped or abducted such person with the same intention or knowledge, or for the same purpose as that with or for which he conceals or detains such person in confinement.
ingredients: Knowledge that the person has been kidnapped or abducted
Wrongfully conceals OR confines such person

punishment_options.type: Same punishment as the original kidnapper/abductor
punishment_options.condition: Punishment mirrors the purpose/intention with which the person is concealed or confined — e.g., if concealed to facilitate murder, punished as per Section 364

sections.key_principle: Extends criminal liability to accessories-after-the-fact who knowingly harbour or conceal kidnapped persons. Punishment is dynamic — it tracks the purpose of concealment/confinement rather than the original act, so a person who conceals a kidnapped victim to enable ransom is punished as per Section 364A, not the base Section 363.

sections.heading: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years with intent to steal from its person
sections.text: Whoever kidnaps or abducts any child under the age of ten years with the intention of taking dishonestly any movable property from the person of such child, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Kidnaps or abducts a child under ten years of age
With intention of dishonestly taking any movable property from the person of such child

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Specific provision targeting child kidnapping motivated by theft (e.g., stealing jewellery worn by the child). Both kidnapping and abduction are covered. The dishonest intention to steal from the child's person must exist at the time of the taking — subsequent intent insufficient.

sections.heading: Trafficking of person
sections.text: Whoever, for the purpose of exploitation, recruits, transports, harbours, transfers, or receives a person or persons by using threats, or using force or any other form of coercion, or by abduction, or by practising fraud or deception, or by abuse of power, or by inducement including giving or receiving payments or benefits to achieve the consent of any person having control over the person recruited, transported, harboured, transferred or received, commits the offence of trafficking. The consent of the victim is immaterial in determination of the offence of trafficking. Punishment ranges from seven years to life imprisonment depending on number of victims and involvement of minors; a public servant or police officer involved in trafficking shall be punished with imprisonment for the remainder of their natural life.
ingredients: For the purpose of exploitation
Recruits, transports, harbours, transfers, or receives a person
By any of: threats, force/coercion, abduction, fraud/deception, abuse of power, inducement/payments to a person having control

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 7 years, up to 10 years, plus fine — base offence
Not less than 10 years, up to life — where more than one person trafficked
Not less than 10 years, up to life — where victim is a minor
Not less than 14 years, up to life — where more than one minor trafficked

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life)
punishment_options.condition: For repeat conviction of minor trafficking, or where public servant/police officer involved

sections.key_principle: Comprehensive anti-trafficking provision substituted by Act 13 of 2013. 'Exploitation' includes physical exploitation, sexual exploitation, slavery or similar practices, servitude, and forced removal of organs. Consent of the victim is expressly declared immaterial. The section applies regardless of whether exploitation actually occurred — the act of trafficking itself is the offence.
sections.amendment_note: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 8, for section 370 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

explanations.explanation_text: The expression 'exploitation' shall include any act of physical exploitation or any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, or the forced removal of organs.
The consent of the victim is immaterial in determination of the offence of trafficking.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 8, for section 370 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Exploitation of a trafficked person
sections.text: Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a minor has been trafficked, engages such minor for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than five years, but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Whoever, knowingly or having reason to believe that a person has been trafficked, engages such person for sexual exploitation in any manner, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years, but which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Knowingly or having reason to believe the person has been trafficked
Engages such person (minor or adult) for sexual exploitation in any manner

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 5 years, up to 7 years, plus fine — where victim is a trafficked minor
Not less than 3 years, up to 5 years, plus fine — where victim is a trafficked adult

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013 to target the demand side of trafficking — the end-user/exploiter. 'Reason to believe' standard is objective; wilful blindness to trafficking indicators is insufficient to escape liability. Operates alongside Section 370 (the trafficker's liability).
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 8 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Habitual dealing in slaves
sections.text: Whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics or deals in slaves, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Habitually (repeated course of conduct)
Imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics, or deals in slaves

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine — alternative

sections.key_principle: The word 'habitually' is the defining element — a single transaction is insufficient; a course of dealing is required. Now largely superseded in practice by Section 370 (trafficking), which is broader in scope, does not require habituality, and carries mandatory minimums.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Selling minor for purposes of prostitution, etc.
sections.text: Whoever sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of any person under the age of eighteen years with intent that such person shall at any age be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person or for any unlawful and immoral purpose, or knowing it to be likely that such person will at any age be employed or used for any such purpose, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of a person under 18 years
With intent/knowledge that the person will be employed for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful and immoral purpose

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Explanation I creates a statutory presumption: disposing of a female under 18 to a prostitute or brothel-keeper is presumed to be with intent for prostitution until the contrary is proved. 'At any age' means intent that the minor will be used for such purposes in the future is sufficient — no immediacy required.

explanations.explanation_text: When a female under the age of eighteen years is sold, let for hire, or otherwise disposed of to a prostitute or to any person who keeps or manages a brothel, the person so disposing of such female shall, until the contrary is proved, be presumed to have disposed of her with the intent that she shall be used for the purpose of prostitution.

For the purposes of this section, 'illicit intercourse' means sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any union or tie which, though not amounting to a marriage, is recognised by the personal law or custom of the community to which they belong or, where they belong to different communities, of both such communities, as constituting between them a quasi-marital relation.

footnotes.note_text: Explanation I and Explanation II added by Act 18 of 1924, s. 3.
Substituted by Act 18 of 1924, s. 2, for certain words.

sections.heading: Buying minor for purposes of prostitution, etc.
sections.text: Whoever buys, hires or otherwise obtains possession of any person under the age of eighteen years with intent that such person shall at any age be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person or for any unlawful and immoral purpose, or knowing it to be likely that such person will at any age be employed or used for any such purpose, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Buys, hires, or otherwise obtains possession of a person under 18 years
With intent/knowledge that the person will be used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or unlawful/immoral purpose

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Mirrors Section 372 from the buyer's side. Explanation I creates a presumption against any prostitute or brothel-keeper who acquires possession of a female under 18. 'Illicit intercourse' has the same meaning as in Section 372 (Explanation II). Together with Section 372, these provisions cover the full chain of commercial sexual exploitation of minors.

explanations.explanation_text: Any prostitute or any person keeping or managing a brothel, who buys, hires or otherwise obtains possession of a female under the age of eighteen years shall, until the contrary is proved, be presumed to have obtained possession of such female with the intent that she shall be used for the purpose of prostitution.
'Illicit intercourse' has the same meaning as in section 372.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 18 of 1924, s. 2, for certain words.
Explanation I and II added by Act 18 of 1924, s. 4.

sections.heading: Unlawful compulsory labour
sections.text: Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Unlawfully compels any person
To labour against that person's will
sections.key_principle: The lightest punishment in the kidnapping/slavery chapter — targets simple forced labour without the trafficking aggravations. 'Unlawfully' distinguishes it from lawful compulsion (e.g., prison labour). In practice, bonded labour cases are prosecuted under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 rather than this provision.

sections.heading: Rape
sections.text: A man is said to commit 'rape' if he penetrates his penis into the vagina, mouth, urethra or anus of a woman or makes her do so; or inserts any object or part of the body (not the penis) into the vagina, urethra or anus; or manipulates any part of a woman's body to cause penetration; or applies his mouth to the vagina, anus or urethra of a woman, under any of seven circumstances: (First) Against her will; (Second) Without her consent; (Third) With consent obtained by putting her in fear of death or hurt; (Fourth) With consent when the man knows he is not her husband and she believes he is; (Fifth) With consent when she is unable to understand the nature of consent due to unsoundness of mind, intoxication or stupefying substance; (Sixth) With or without consent when she is under eighteen years of age; (Seventh) When she is unable to communicate consent. Exception 1: Medical procedures do not constitute rape. Exception 2: Sexual intercourse by a man with his wife, the wife not being under fifteen years of age, is not rape.
ingredients: A man (perpetrator must be male)

Any of four acts: penile penetration into vagina/mouth/urethra/anus; insertion of object/body part into vagina/urethra/anus; manipulation causing penetration; application of mouth to vagina/anus/urethra of a woman

Under any of seven circumstances: against will; without consent; consent by fear of death/hurt; consent by identity fraud; consent vitiated by unsoundness of mind/intoxication; victim under 18; unable to communicate consent
sections.key_principle: Comprehensively substituted by Act 13 of 2013 following the December 2012 gang rape case. Expanded definition to include oral rape, object insertion, and digital penetration. Consent defined as unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures or non-verbal communication. Absence of physical resistance does not imply consent. Marital rape exception retained but restricted — wife must be 15 or older (not 18).
sections.amendment_note: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 9, for sections 375, 376, 376A, 376B, 376C and 376D (w.e.f. 3-2-2013). Sub-section (3) of Section 376 (punishment for rape of woman under 16) inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

explanations.explanation_text: For the purposes of this section, 'vagina' shall also include labia majora.

Consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement when the woman by words, gestures or any form of verbal or non-verbal communication, communicates willingness to participate in the specific sexual act. A woman who does not physically resist to the act of penetration shall not by reason only of that fact be regarded as consenting to the sexual activity.

exceptions: Exception 1: A medical procedure or intervention shall not constitute rape.
Exception 2: Sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under fifteen years of age, is not rape.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 43 of 1983, s. 3, for the heading 'Of rape' and ss. 375 and 376.
Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 9, for sections 375, 376, 376A, 376B, 376C and 376D (w.e.f. 03-02-2013).

sections.heading: Punishment for rape
sections.text: Whoever, except in the cases provided for in sub-section (2), commits rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Sub-section (2) provides enhanced punishment (rigorous imprisonment not less than ten years up to life, meaning remainder of natural life, plus fine) for aggravated rape by police officers, public servants, armed forces members, prison staff, hospital staff, relatives/guardians/teachers, during communal violence, of pregnant women, of women incapable of consenting, by persons in dominance, of mentally/physically disabled women, causing grievous hurt/maiming, or repeat rape. Sub-section (3): rape of woman under sixteen — not less than twenty years up to life, plus fine paid to victim.
ingredients: Commits rape as defined in Section 375

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 10 years, up to imprisonment for life, plus fine — basic offence (sub-section 1)
Not less than 10 years, up to life (remainder of natural life), plus fine — aggravated categories under sub-section (2)
Not less than 20 years, up to life (remainder of natural life), plus fine paid to victim — rape of woman under 16 (sub-section 3)

sections.key_principle: Mandatory minimum of 10 years introduced by Act 13 of 2013. 'Imprisonment for life' in sub-section (2) means imprisonment for the remainder of the person's natural life — not a fixed term. Fine is mandatory and, in sub-section (3) cases, must be paid to the victim for medical expenses and rehabilitation. Sub-section (3) inserted by Act 22 of 2018 following the Kathua and Unnao cases.
sections.amendment_note: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013. Sub-section (3) inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018). Clause (i) of sub-section (2) omitted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018). Minimum punishment raised from 7 years to 10 years by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4, for 'shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine' (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).
Clause (i) omitted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 4 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

sections.heading: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim
sections.text: Whoever, commits an offence punishable under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) of section 376 and in the course of such commission inflicts an injury which causes the death of the woman or causes the woman to be in a persistent vegetative state, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, or with death.
ingredients: Commits rape punishable under Section 376(1) or 376(2)
In the course of such commission inflicts injury causing death of the woman OR causing persistent vegetative state

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 20 years, up to life (remainder of natural life)

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013 to address cases like the December 2012 Delhi gang rape. 'Persistent vegetative state' is a specific medical condition — permanent unconsciousness — and its inclusion ensures parity of punishment with cases resulting in death. The injury causing death/vegetative state must occur in the course of committing rape.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 9 (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Punishment for rape on woman under twelve years of age
sections.text: Whoever commits rape on a woman under twelve years of age shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine or with death. Such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and shall be paid to the victim.
ingredients: Commits rape (as defined in Section 375)
Victim is a woman under twelve years of age

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 20 years, up to life (remainder of natural life), plus fine paid to victim
In the gravest cases, in addition to or instead of life imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018 following nationwide outrage at child rapes. Fine is mandatory and must be paid to the victim for medical expenses and rehabilitation. The age threshold (12) is lower than Section 376(3) (16 years), attracting death as a possible punishment.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 5 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 5 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

sections.heading: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation
sections.text: Whoever has sexual intercourse with his own wife, who is living separately, whether under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than two years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Sexual intercourse by a husband with his own wife
Wife is living separately — under a decree of separation or otherwise
Without her consent

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 2 years, up to 7 years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Partial inroad into marital rape immunity — covers only the situation of separation. 'Living separately otherwise' is broader than formal decree and includes informal separation. 'Sexual intercourse' means any of the acts in clauses (a) to (d) of Section 375 — not merely penile-vaginal intercourse. Section 376 Exception 2 (marital rape exception) continues to apply where the couple is cohabiting.

explanations.explanation_text: In this section, 'sexual intercourse' shall mean any of the acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of section 375.

sections.heading: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority
sections.text: Whoever, being in a position of authority or fiduciary relationship, or a public servant, or superintendent/manager of a jail or women's/children's institution, or on the management/staff of a hospital, abuses such position or fiduciary relationship to induce or seduce any woman in custody or under charge or present in the premises to have sexual intercourse with him, such sexual intercourse not amounting to rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment not less than five years, up to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Being in a position of authority/fiduciary relationship, OR public servant, OR jail/institution superintendent, OR hospital management/staff
Abuses such position to induce or seduce a woman in custody/under charge/in premises
To have sexual intercourse — not amounting to rape (which would be Section 376)

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 5 years, up to 10 years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Targets coercive sexual exploitation by authority figures where consent appears formally present but is vitiated by power imbalance. 'Not amounting to rape' is the key qualifier — if force or complete absence of consent is established, Section 376 applies instead. Covers police officers, doctors, teachers, prison officials, and others in positions of trust.

explanations.explanation_text: In this section, 'sexual intercourse' shall mean any of the acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of section 375.
For the purposes of this section, Explanation 1 to section 375 shall also be applicable.

'Superintendent', in relation to a jail, remand home or other place of custody or a women's or children's institution, includes a person holding any other office in such jail, remand home, place or institution by virtue of which such person can exercise any authority or control over its inmates.
The expressions 'hospital' and 'women's or children's institution' shall respectively have the same meaning as in Explanation to sub-section (2) of section 376.

sections.heading: Gang rape
sections.text: Where a woman is raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons shall be deemed to have committed the offence of rape and shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine. Such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and shall be paid to the victim.
ingredients: A woman is raped
By one or more persons constituting a group OR acting in furtherance of a common intention

punishment_options.condition: Not less than 20 years, up to life (remainder of natural life), plus fine paid to victim

sections.key_principle: Each member of the group is deemed to have committed rape regardless of their individual act — collective liability based on common intention. Even a member who did not personally commit the act of rape is punished as if they did. Fine is mandatory and must be paid to the victim.

sections.heading: Punishment for gang rape on woman under sixteen years of age
sections.text: Where a woman under sixteen years of age is raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons shall be deemed to have committed the offence of rape and shall be punished with imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine. Such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and shall be paid to the victim.
ingredients: Victim is a woman under sixteen years of age
Raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life)
punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — plus fine paid to victim

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018. Life imprisonment (full natural life) is mandatory — there is no discretion to impose a shorter term. Stricter than Section 376D (gang rape of adult woman) where 20 years minimum applies but life is not mandatory.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 6 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 6 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

sections.heading: Punishment for gang rape on woman under twelve years of age
sections.text: Where a woman under twelve years of age is raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons shall be deemed to have committed the offence of rape and shall be punished with imprisonment for life, which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, and with fine, or with death. Such fine shall be just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and shall be paid to the victim.
ingredients: Victim is a woman under twelve years of age
Raped by one or more persons constituting a group or acting in furtherance of a common intention

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life)

punishment_options.condition: In the gravest cases, as an alternative to life imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018. The most severe gang rape provision — death penalty is available as an option alongside mandatory life imprisonment. The fine must be paid to the victim for rehabilitation.
sections.amendment_note: Inserted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 6 (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

sections.heading: Punishment for repeat offenders
sections.text: Whoever has been previously convicted of an offence punishable under section 376 or section 376A or section 376AB or section 376D or section 376DA or section 376DB, and is subsequently convicted of an offence punishable under any of the said sections shall be punished with imprisonment for life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life, or with death.
ingredients: Previous conviction under Section 376, 376A, 376AB, 376D, 376DA, or 376DB
Subsequent conviction under any of the said sections

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment for life (remainder of natural life)

punishment_options.condition: In the gravest cases — alternative to life imprisonment

sections.key_principle: Recidivist provision — mandatory life imprisonment or death for any second conviction under the listed rape sections. There is no discretion to award a lesser sentence. Cross-reference updated by Act 22 of 2018 to include sections 376AB, 376DA, and 376DB.
sections.amendment_note: Substituted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 7, for 'section 376D' (w.e.f. 21-4-2018) — reference expanded to include 376AB, 376DA, and 376DB.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 22 of 2018, s. 7, for 'section 376D' (w.e.f. 21-4-2018).

sections.heading: Unnatural offences
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily has carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any man, woman or animal, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Explanation: Penetration is sufficient to constitute the carnal intercourse necessary to the offence described in this section.
ingredients: Voluntarily has carnal intercourse
Against the order of nature
With any man, woman, or animal
Penetration is sufficient

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine — alternative

sections.key_principle: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court read down Section 377 to decriminalise consensual same-sex intercourse between adults — holding it unconstitutional to the extent it criminalised consensual acts between adults. Section 377 continues to apply to: non-consensual acts between adults, acts involving minors, and bestiality. The section has not been formally amended or deleted.

explanations.explanation_text: Penetration is sufficient to constitute the carnal intercourse necessary to the offence described in this section.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Theft
sections.text: Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.
ingredients: Dishonest intention to take movable property
Out of the possession of any person
Without that person's consent
Moving the property in order to such taking (any movement, however slight, suffices)
sections.key_principle: Five elements: (1) dishonest intention; (2) movable property; (3) out of possession of another; (4) without consent; (5) actual movement. Theft is complete on the slightest movement — asportation doctrine. Consent obtained by fraud is not valid consent. A thing attached to the earth is not movable property but becomes so on severance. Illustrations (a)–(p) enumerate detailed scenarios distinguishing theft from non-theft.
illustrations: A cuts down a tree on Z's ground with intent to take it — theft complete as soon as tree is severed.
A puts a bait in his pocket to induce Z's dog to follow — theft when dog begins to follow.
A drives Z's bullock to take the treasure it carries — theft when bullock begins to move.
Z's servant A runs away with Z's plate without consent — theft.
A asks charity from Z's wife who gives A money belonging to Z — no theft if A believes wife was authorised.

explanations.explanation_text: A thing so long as it is attached to the earth is not movable property; it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth.
A moving effected by the same act which effects the severance may be a theft.
A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it.
A person who by any means causes an animal to move is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal.
The consent mentioned in the definition may be express or implied, and may be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied.

sections.heading: Punishment for theft
sections.text: Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commits theft as defined in Section 378
sections.key_principle: Base punishment for simple theft. Cognizable, bailable offence. Aggravated forms carry higher punishment: Section 380 (theft in dwelling), Section 381 (theft by servant), Section 382 (theft with preparation for violence).

sections.heading: Theft in dwelling house, etc.
sections.text: Whoever commits theft in any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or used for the custody of property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commits theft (Section 378)
In a building, tent, or vessel
Used as a human dwelling OR used for the custody of property

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: The aggravation is the location — a place of habitation or property custody. 'Tent' includes temporary shelters; 'vessel' includes boats used as dwellings. A building 'used for custody of property' includes warehouses, godowns, and lockers even if not inhabited. Fine is mandatory (in addition to imprisonment).

sections.heading: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master
sections.text: Whoever, being a clerk or servant, or being employed in the capacity of a clerk or servant, commits theft in respect of any property in the possession of his master or employer, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Being a clerk, servant, or employed in such capacity
Commits theft of property in the possession of the master/employer

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: The aggravation is the breach of trust inherent in the employer-employee relationship. 'In possession of master' does not require physical possession by the master at the moment of theft — constructive possession suffices. Overlaps with criminal breach of trust (Section 406) but differs in that theft requires asportation (movement) and no element of entrustment.

sections.heading: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to the committing of the theft
sections.text: Whoever commits theft, having made preparation for causing death, or hurt, or restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of restraint, to any person, in order to the committing of such theft, or in order to the effecting of his escape after the committing of such theft, or in order to the retaining of property taken by such theft, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commits theft (Section 378)
Having made preparation for causing death, hurt, restraint, or fear thereof
Such preparation in order to: commit the theft, OR effect escape after theft, OR retain property taken

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: The preparation for violence is the aggravating factor — actual violence need not occur; mere preparation is sufficient. Three purposes bring the preparation within the section: committing the theft, effecting escape, or retaining the stolen property. Punishment is rigorous (not simple) imprisonment only.
illustrations: A commits theft with a loaded pistol under his garment intending to hurt Z if resisted — offence made out.
A picks Z's pocket having posted companions to restrain Z if he perceives and resists — offence made out.

sections.heading: Extortion
sections.text: Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to any person any property, or valuable security or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable security, commits 'extortion'.
ingredients: Intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury (to that person or any other)
Thereby dishonestly induces that person to deliver to any person
