Property, OR valuable security, OR anything signed/sealed convertible into a valuable security
sections.key_principle: Extortion requires: (1) putting a person in fear of injury; (2) a causal link — the fear must induce the delivery; (3) the delivery must be to 'any person' — not necessarily the extortionist. Injury is broadly defined (Section 44) to include any harm to body, mind, reputation, or property. Threats to third parties (family members) suffice. Distinguished from robbery: in extortion, the victim 'consents' (albeit under duress) and delivers; in robbery, the offender directly takes.
illustrations: A threatens to publish a defamatory libel against Z unless Z gives money — extortion.
A threatens to keep Z's child in wrongful confinement unless Z signs a promissory note — extortion.
A threatens to send club-men to plough Z's field unless Z delivers a bond to B — extortion.
A, by putting Z in fear of grievous hurt, induces Z to sign a blank paper — extortion (paper may be converted to valuable security).

sections.heading: Punishment for extortion
sections.text: Whoever commits extortion shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commits extortion as defined in Section 383
sections.key_principle: Base punishment for simple extortion — identical maximum to theft (Section 379). Aggravated forms under Sections 385–389 carry higher punishments depending on the nature of the fear employed.

sections.heading: Putting person in fear of injury in order to commit extortion
sections.text: Whoever, in order to the committing of extortion, puts any person in fear, or attempts to put any person in fear, of any injury, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Puts or attempts to put any person in fear of any injury
In order to commit extortion
sections.key_principle: Attempt provision — covers the threat/intimidation stage before the delivery of property. The delivery of property need not occur for this section to apply; an attempt to put in fear suffices. Lighter than Section 384 (completed extortion) — the maximum is 2 years vs 3 years.

sections.heading: Extortion by putting a person in fear of death or grievous hurt
sections.text: Whoever commits extortion by putting any person in fear of death or of grievous hurt to that person or to any other, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commits extortion (Section 383)
By putting any person in fear of death or grievous hurt — to that person or any other

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Aggravated extortion where the fear used is of death or grievous hurt (Section 320). Tripling of the base 3-year maximum to 10 years reflects the severity of the threat. The threat may be directed at the victim or at any third party.

sections.heading: Putting person in fear of death or of grievous hurt, in order to commit extortion
sections.text: Whoever, in order to the committing of extortion, puts or attempts to put any person in fear of death or of grievous hurt to that person or to any other, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Puts or attempts to put any person in fear of death or grievous hurt
In order to commit extortion (delivery of property not required)

punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, plus fine

sections.key_principle: Attempt counterpart to Section 386 — covers the threat stage without completed delivery. Mirrors the Section 385/384 relationship but at the aggravated (death/grievous hurt) threat level. Seven years maximum (vs ten in Section 386 for completed offence).

sections.heading: Extortion by threat of accusation of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, etc.
sections.text: Whoever commits extortion by putting any person in fear of an accusation against that person or any other, of having committed or attempted to commit any offence punishable with death, or with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, or of having attempted to induce any other person to commit such offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if the offence be one punishable under section 377 of this Code, may be punished with imprisonment for life.
ingredients: Commits extortion

By putting a person in fear of accusation — of themselves or another — of having committed/attempted any offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or up to 10 years; OR of having attempted to induce another to commit such offence

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine
If the accusation is of an offence under Section 377 (unnatural offences)

sections.key_principle: Blackmail provision — the 'injury' is the threat of a serious criminal accusation. Section 377 reference (now partially read down) reflects the historical use of sodomy accusations for blackmail. The accusation need not be true; threatening a false accusation of a serious offence to extort property is the classic blackmail scenario.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Putting person in fear or accusation of offence, in order to commit extortion
sections.text: Whoever, in order to the committing of extortion, puts or attempts to put any person in fear of an accusation, against that person or any other, of having committed, or attempted to commit, an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the offence be punishable under section 377 of this Code, may be punished with imprisonment for life.
ingredients: Puts or attempts to put any person in fear of accusation of a serious offence
In order to commit extortion (delivery of property not required)

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine
If the accusation relates to an offence under Section 377

sections.key_principle: Attempt counterpart to Section 388 — the threat/blackmail attempt stage without completed delivery. Unusually, the maximum (10 years) is the same as for the completed offence (Section 388), reflecting the seriousness of the attempt itself.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Robbery
sections.text: In all robbery there is either theft or extortion. Theft is 'robbery' if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. Extortion is 'robbery' if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted. The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.
ingredients: Theft-robbery: theft (Section 378) + voluntarily causes/attempts to cause death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear of instant versions thereof, for that end
Extortion-robbery: extortion (Section 383) + offender's presence + instant fear of death/hurt/wrongful restraint + immediate delivery on the spot
sections.key_principle: Robbery is an aggravated form of theft or extortion — the additional element is actual or attempted violence (or its apprehension). Three time-points trigger theft-robbery: during commission, during carrying away, or during attempt to carry away. For extortion-robbery: (1) presence of offender; (2) fear must be of instant harm; (3) delivery must be on the spot. 'Instant' is the critical qualifier — a threat of future harm converts extortion but not robbery. Punishment under Section 392. Punishment under Section 393 (attempt to commit robbery).

explanations.explanation_text: The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Against Property

sections.heading: Dacoity
sections.text: When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit a robbery, or where the whole number of persons conjointly committing or attempting to commit a robbery, and persons present and aiding such commission or attempt, amount to five or more, every person so committing, attempting or aiding, is said to commit "dacoity".
ingredients: Five or more persons acting conjointly
Committing or attempting to commit robbery; OR
Persons committing/attempting + persons present and aiding together amount to five or more
Every such person is said to commit dacoity
sections.key_principle: The gravamen is the conjoint number — five or more persons in aggregate (including those merely present and aiding). Each such person is equally liable, regardless of their individual role.

sections.heading: Punishment for robbery
sections.text: Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.

punishment_options.condition: Up to ten years, plus fine
Up to fourteen years if robbery is committed on a highway between sunset and sunrise

sections.key_principle: Robbery on a highway at night attracts an enhanced maximum — fourteen years instead of ten — reflecting the heightened danger to travellers.

sections.heading: Attempt to commit robbery
sections.text: Whoever attempts to commit robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: Attempt to commit robbery is a standalone offence; the maximum of seven years is lower than the ten-year ceiling for completed robbery under Section 392.

sections.heading: Voluntarily causing hurt in committing robbery
sections.text: If any person, in committing or in attempting to commit robbery, voluntarily causes hurt, such person, and any other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting to commit such robbery, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: Joint liability — all persons jointly concerned in the robbery are equally liable for the enhanced punishment, even if only one of them actually caused the hurt.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Punishment for dacoity
sections.text: Whoever commits dacoity shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Dacoity with murder
sections.text: If any one of five or more persons, who are conjointly committing dacoity, commits murder in so committing dacoity, every one of those persons shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: Constructive joint liability — even if only one member of the dacoity gang commits murder, every member of the gang is equally liable for the murder. This is among the most severe applications of joint liability in the IPC.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt
sections.text: If, at the time of committing robbery or dacoity, the offender uses any deadly weapon, or causes grievous hurt to any person, or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt to any person, the imprisonment with which such offender shall be punished shall not be less than seven years.

punishment_options.condition: Not less than seven years — applies where deadly weapon is used, or grievous hurt is caused, or death/grievous hurt is attempted during robbery or dacoity

sections.key_principle: Section 397 imposes a mandatory minimum sentence of seven years — the court has no discretion to award less — where deadly weapons are used or grievous hurt caused during robbery or dacoity.

sections.heading: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon
sections.text: If, at the time of attempting to commit robbery or dacoity, the offender is armed with any deadly weapon, the imprisonment with which such offender shall be punished shall not be less than seven years.

punishment_options.condition: Not less than seven years — applies where offender is armed with a deadly weapon at the time of attempt

sections.key_principle: Unlike Section 397 (which requires actual use of weapon or causing of grievous hurt), Section 398 is triggered merely by being armed at the time of attempt — mere possession of a deadly weapon during the attempt suffices for the mandatory minimum.

sections.heading: Making preparation to commit dacoity
sections.text: Whoever makes any preparation for committing dacoity, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: Uniquely, Section 399 punishes the preparatory stage itself — unlike most offences where preparation is not separately punishable — reflecting the legislature's intent to nip dacoity conspiracies at an early stage.

sections.heading: Punishment for belonging to gang of dacoits
sections.text: Whoever, at any time after the passing of this Act, shall belong to a gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing dacoity, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Belonging to a gang of persons
Gang associated for the purpose of habitually committing dacoity
sections.key_principle: Mere membership of a gang habitually engaged in dacoity is the offence — no specific act of dacoity need be proved against the individual.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Punishment for belonging to gang of thieves
sections.text: Whoever, at any time after the passing of this Act, shall belong to any wandering or other gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing theft or robbery, and not being a gang of thugs or dacoits, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Belonging to a wandering or other gang
Gang associated for habitually committing theft or robbery
The gang must NOT be a gang of thugs or dacoits (those attract Sections 400 and higher)
sections.key_principle: Section 401 covers habitual theft/robbery gangs that fall short of dacoity gangs; the lower ceiling (seven years) reflects their lesser danger compared to dacoity gangs under Section 400.

sections.heading: Assembling for purpose of committing dacoity
sections.text: Whoever, at any time after the passing of this Act, shall be one of five or more persons assembled for the purpose of committing dacoity, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Being one of five or more persons
Assembled for the purpose of committing dacoity
sections.key_principle: Section 402 targets assembly with intent — analogous to Section 399 (preparation) but focused on the act of assembling in a group of five or more. No overt act of dacoity need have commenced.

sections.heading: Dishonest misappropriation of property
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use any movable property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Dishonest misappropriation or conversion
Of movable property
To accused's own use

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest intention to misappropriate or convert movable property to own use

sections.key_principle: Unlike theft, criminal misappropriation does not require the initial taking to be wrongful — the dishonest appropriation at a later stage (e.g., after innocent finding) constitutes the offence.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A takes property belonging to Z out of Z's possession, in good faith believing at the time when he takes it, that the property belongs to himself. A is not guilty of theft; but if A, after discovering his mistake, dishonestly appropriates the property to his own use, he is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: A subsequent dishonest appropriation after an innocent taking constitutes criminal misappropriation.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, being on friendly terms with Z, goes into Z's library in Z's absence, and takes away a book without Z's express consent. Here, if A was under the impression that he had Z's implied consent to take the book for the purpose of reading it, A has not committed theft. But, if A afterwards sells the book for his own benefit, he is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Selling property taken under implied consent, for personal benefit, constitutes dishonest misappropriation.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A and B, being joint owners of a horse, A takes the horse out of B's possession, intending to use it. Here, as A has a right to use the horse, he does not dishonestly misappropriate it. But, if A sells the horse and appropriates the whole proceeds to his own use, he is guilty of an offence under this section.
illustrations.verdict: Guilty under Section 403 (for selling and keeping proceeds)
illustrations.key_principle: A joint owner who sells jointly-owned property and keeps all proceeds dishonestly misappropriates the other owner's share.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A dishonest misappropriation for a time only is a misappropriation within the meaning of this section.
explanations.plain_language: Even temporary dishonest appropriation — intending to return the property later — constitutes the offence.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: A person who finds property not in the possession of any other person, and takes such property for the purpose of protecting it for, or of restoring it to, the owner, does not take or misappropriate it dishonestly, and is not guilty of an offence; but he is guilty of the offence above defined, if he appropriates it to his own use, when he knows or has the means of discovering the owner, or before he has used reasonable means to discover and give notice to the owner and has kept the property a reasonable time to enable the owner to claim it.
explanations.plain_language: A finder of lost property is not guilty if they take it to protect/return it. They become guilty if they appropriate it knowing who the owner is, or without making reasonable effort to find the owner.

sections.heading: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use property, knowing that such property was in the possession of a deceased person at the time of that person's decease, and has not since been in the possession of any person legally entitled to such possession, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine, and if the offender at the time of such person's decease was employed by him as a clerk or servant, the imprisonment may extend to seven years.
ingredients: Dishonest misappropriation or conversion to own use
Of property that was in possession of a deceased person at the time of death
Property has not since come into the possession of any person legally entitled to it
Knowledge of the above circumstances

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years, plus fine
Up to seven years if offender was employed as a clerk or servant of the deceased at the time of death

sections.key_principle: This section protects the estate of a deceased person during the interval before legal heirs take possession. The enhanced punishment for clerks/servants reflects the aggravated breach of trust involved.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: Z dies in possession of furniture and money. His servant A, before the money comes into the possession of any person entitled to such possession, dishonestly misappropriates it. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.verdict: Guilty under Section 404 (enhanced punishment as servant)
illustrations.key_principle: A servant who misappropriates the deceased employer's property before heirs take possession is guilty under the aggravated limb of Section 404.

sections.heading: Criminal breach of trust
sections.text: Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits "criminal breach of trust".
ingredients: Entrustment of property or dominion over property
Dishonest misappropriation or conversion to own use; OR
Dishonest use or disposal in violation of any law or legal contract governing the trust; OR
Wilfully suffering any other person to do the above
sections.key_distinction_from_s403: Section 403 (criminal misappropriation) does not require prior entrustment; Section 405 (criminal breach of trust) is premised on a pre-existing relationship of trust and entrustment. The betrayal of that trust is the gravamen.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A person, being an employer of an establishment (whether exempted under section 17 of the Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 or not) who deducts the employee's contribution from the wages payable to the employee for credit to a Provident Fund or Family Pension Fund established by any law for the time being in force, shall be deemed to have been entrusted with the amount of the contribution so deducted by him and if he makes default in the payment of such contribution to the said Fund in violation of the said law, shall be deemed to have dishonestly used the amount of the said contribution in violation of a direction of law as aforesaid.
explanations.plain_language: An employer who deducts PF contributions from wages but fails to deposit them is deemed to have been entrusted with those amounts and to have dishonestly misused them.
explanations.inserted_by: Act 40 of 1973, s. 9 (w.e.f. 1-11-1973); Explanation numbered as Explanation 1 by Act 38 of 1975, s. 9; words amended by Act 33 of 1988, s. 27

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: A person, being an employer, who deducts the employees' contribution from the wages payable to the employee for credit to the Employees' State Insurance Fund held and administered by the Employees' State Insurance Corporation established under the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948 (34 of 1948), shall be deemed to have been entrusted with the amount of the contribution so deducted by him and if he makes default in the payment of such contribution to the said Fund in violation of the said Act, shall be deemed to have dishonestly used the amount of the said contribution in violation of a direction of law as aforesaid.
explanations.plain_language: Same principle extended to ESI contributions — an employer deducting ESI contributions but defaulting on payment to the ESIC Fund is deemed to have committed criminal breach of trust.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, being executor to the will of a deceased person, dishonestly disobeys the law which directs him to divide the effects according to the will, and appropriates them to his own use. A has committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.key_principle: An executor who diverts estate assets to personal use in breach of testamentary duty commits criminal breach of trust.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A is a warehouse-keeper. Z going on a journey, entrusts his furniture to A, under a contract that it shall be returned on payment of a stipulated sum for warehouse room. A dishonestly sells the goods. A has committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.key_principle: A bailee (warehouse-keeper) who sells entrusted goods is in criminal breach of trust.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, residing in Calcutta, is agent for Z, residing at Delhi. There is an express or implied contract between A and Z, that all sums remitted by Z to A shall be invested by A, according to Z's direction. Z remits a lakh of rupees to A, with directions to A to invest the same in Company's paper. A dishonestly disobeys the directions and employs the money in his own business. A has committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.key_principle: An agent who diverts principal's funds to personal business in defiance of express instructions commits criminal breach of trust.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: But if A, in the last illustration, not dishonestly but in good faith, believing that it will be more for Z's advantage to hold shares in the Bank of Bengal, disobeys Z's directions, and buys shares in the Bank of Bengal, for Z, instead of buying Company's paper, here, though Z should suffer loss, and should be entitled to bring a civil action against A, on account of that loss, yet A, not having acted dishonestly, has not committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.verdict: NOT criminal breach of trust — only civil liability
illustrations.key_principle: Good faith disobedience of instructions (no dishonest intent) does not constitute criminal breach of trust, even if the principal suffers loss — dishonesty is the essential element.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A, a revenue-officer, is entrusted with public money and is either directed by law, or bound by a contract, express or implied, with the Government, to pay into a certain treasury all the public money which he holds. A dishonestly appropriates the money. A has committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.key_principle: A public servant who misappropriates entrusted public funds commits criminal breach of trust, also triggering the aggravated provision of Section 409.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f)
illustrations.text: A, a carrier, is entrusted by Z with property to be carried by land or by water. A dishonestly misappropriates the property. A has committed criminal breach of trust.
illustrations.verdict: Criminal breach of trust (also attracts Section 407 as carrier)
illustrations.key_principle: A carrier who misappropriates goods entrusted for transport commits criminal breach of trust, attracting the aggravated punishment under Section 407.

Explanation numbered as Explanation 1 by Act 38 of 1975, s. 9 (w.e.f. 1-9-1975).
Words inserted by Act 33 of 1988, s. 27 (w.e.f. 1-8-1988).
Explanation 2 inserted by Act 38 of 1975, s. 9 (w.e.f. 1-9-1975).

sections.heading: Punishment for criminal breach of trust
sections.text: Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Section 406 is the general punishment for criminal breach of trust (Section 405). Aggravated versions — by carriers (407), clerks/servants (408), and public servants/bankers (409) — carry higher punishments.

sections.heading: Criminal breach of trust by carrier, etc.
sections.text: Whoever, being entrusted with property as a carrier, wharfinger or warehouse-keeper, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of such property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: The enhanced punishment (seven years vs. three under Section 406) reflects the public's dependence on carriers and custodians for safe transit and storage of goods.

sections.heading: Criminal breach of trust by clerk or servant
sections.text: Whoever, being a clerk or servant or employed as a clerk or servant, and being in any manner entrusted in such capacity with property, or with any dominion over property, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of that property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
aggravated_categories: Person employed as a clerk or servant
sections.key_principle: The employment relationship creates a heightened duty of fidelity. Breach by a clerk or servant is aggravated because the employer places special confidence in such employees for day-to-day handling of property.

sections.heading: Criminal breach of trust by public servant, or by banker, merchant or agent
sections.text: Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property in his capacity of a public servant or in the way of his business as a banker, merchant, factor, broker, attorney or agent, commits criminal breach of trust in respect of that property, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
sections.key_principle: Section 409 carries the highest punishment for criminal breach of trust — up to life imprisonment — because public servants and commercial fiduciaries (bankers, brokers, etc.) hold positions of the highest public and financial trust.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Stolen property
sections.text: Property, the possession whereof has been transferred by theft, or by extortion, or by robbery, and property which has been criminally misappropriated or in respect of which criminal breach of trust has been committed, is designated as "stolen property", whether the transfer has been made, or the misappropriation or breach of trust has been committed, within or without India. But, if such property subsequently comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to the possession thereof, it then ceases to be stolen property.
sections.sub_heading_context: Of the Receiving of Stolen Property
categories_of_stolen_property: Property whose possession was transferred by theft
Property whose possession was transferred by extortion
Property whose possession was transferred by robbery
Property that has been criminally misappropriated (Section 403/404)
Property in respect of which criminal breach of trust has been committed (Section 405)
sections.territorial_scope: Applies whether the offence occurred within or outside India.
sections.cessation_rule: Property ceases to be 'stolen property' once it comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to possess it.
sections.key_principle: Section 410 provides the foundational definition on which Sections 411–414 (receiving, habitually dealing, and concealing stolen property) depend.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'British India' have successively been substituted by the A.O. 1948, the A.O. 1950 and Act 3 of 1951, s. 3 and the Sch., to read 'India'.

sections.heading: Dishonestly receiving stolen property
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Receiving or retaining stolen property
Dishonestly
Knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen property
sections.key_principle: The phrase 'reason to believe' is objective — it is not enough that the accused did not actually know; if a reasonable person in the circumstances would have believed the property was stolen, the mental element is satisfied.

sections.heading: Dishonestly receiving property stolen in the commission of a dacoity
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, the possession whereof he knows or has reason to believe to have been transferred by the commission of dacoity, or dishonestly receives from a person, whom he knows or has reason to believe to belong or to have belonged to a gang of dacoits, property which he knows or has reason to believe to have been stolen, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Receiving or retaining stolen property knowing or having reason to believe it was stolen in a dacoity; OR
Receiving property from a person known or believed to belong/have belonged to a gang of dacoits, knowing or believing it to be stolen
sections.key_principle: The severe punishment (up to life imprisonment) reflects that receiving dacoity property funds and encourages organised violent crime. Knowledge of the dacoit connection — even inferred from circumstances — suffices.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Habitually dealing in stolen property
sections.text: Whoever habitually receives or deals in property which he knows or has reason to believe to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Habitual receipt or dealing in property
Knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen property
sections.key_principle: Section 413 targets the habitual 'fence' — a person who systematically receives and deals in stolen goods. The element of habituality distinguishes this from the single-act offence under Section 411.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Assisting in concealment of stolen property
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily assists in concealing or disposing of or making away with property which he knows or has reason to believe to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntary assistance in concealing, disposing of, or making away with property
Knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen property
sections.key_principle: Section 414 targets active concealment/disposal assistance, as distinct from mere receipt (Section 411). The voluntariness requirement means accidental or unknowing assistance does not attract liability.

sections.heading: Cheating
sections.text: Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
ingredients: Deception of a person
Fraudulent or dishonest inducement to deliver property or consent to its retention; OR
Intentional inducement to do or omit something the person would not otherwise do/omit
The act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm in body, mind, reputation or property

explanation.label: Explanation
explanation.text: A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section.
explanation.plain_language: Active misrepresentation is not necessary — deliberately hiding material facts is itself deception for the purposes of this section.

sections.key_distinction: Cheating requires both deception AND damage (actual or likely). Mere deception without harm, or harm without deception, does not constitute cheating under this section.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A, by falsely pretending to be in the Civil Service, intentionally deceives Z, and thus dishonestly induces Z to let him have on credit goods for which he does not mean to pay. A cheats.
illustrations.key_principle: False pretence of status to obtain credit goods with no intention to pay is cheating.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A, by putting a counterfeit mark on an article, intentionally deceives Z into a belief that this article was made by a certain celebrated manufacturer, and thus dishonestly induces Z to buy and pay for the article. A cheats.
illustrations.key_principle: Counterfeiting a manufacturer's mark to deceive a buyer as to the article's origin is cheating.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A, by exhibiting to Z a false sample of an article intentionally deceives Z into believing that the article corresponds with the sample, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to buy and pay for the article. A cheats.
illustrations.key_principle: Showing a false sample to induce purchase of inferior goods is cheating.

illustrations.label: Illustration (g)
illustrations.text: A intentionally deceives Z into a belief that A means to deliver to Z a certain quantity of indigo plant which he does not intend to deliver, and thereby dishonestly induces Z to advance money upon the faith of such delivery. A cheats; but if A, at the time of obtaining the money, intends to deliver the indigo plant, and afterwards breaks his contract and does not deliver it, he does not cheat, but is liable only to a civil action for breach of contract.
illustrations.verdict: Cheating (if no intent to deliver from the start); Civil liability only (if intent existed at start)
illustrations.key_principle: The decisive factor is the state of mind AT THE TIME of inducement — a pre-existing dishonest intent is criminal; a subsequent failure to perform is merely a civil wrong.

sections.heading: Cheating by personation
sections.text: A person is said to "cheat by personation" if he cheats by pretending to be some other person, or by knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is.

explanation.label: Explanation
explanation.text: The offence is committed whether the individual personated is a real or imaginary person.
explanation.plain_language: It is immaterial whether the person being impersonated actually exists — pretending to be a fictitious person also constitutes cheating by personation.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A cheats by pretending to be a certain rich banker of the same name. A cheats by personation.
illustrations.key_principle: Impersonating a real person (even one who shares your name) to gain credit or advantage is cheating by personation.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A cheats by pretending to be B, a person who is deceased. A cheats by personation.
illustrations.key_principle: Impersonating a deceased person is cheating by personation — the explanation confirms it need not be a living person.

sections.heading: Punishment for cheating
sections.text: Whoever cheats shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Section 417 is the general punishment for basic cheating under Section 415. Aggravated forms — with property delivery (420), against a person the accused was duty-bound to protect (418), and by personation (419) — attract higher punishments.

sections.heading: Cheating with knowledge that wrongful loss may ensue to person whose interest offender is bound to protect
sections.text: Whoever cheats with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause wrongful loss to a person whose interest in the transaction to which the cheating relates, he was bound, either by law, or by a legal contract, to protect, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Cheating (as defined in Section 415)
Knowledge that the cheating is likely to cause wrongful loss
The person suffering wrongful loss is one whose interest the accused was legally or contractually bound to protect
sections.key_principle: The aggravation here is the breach of a legal or contractual duty to protect the very person being cheated — e.g., an agent cheating his principal, a trustee cheating a beneficiary. The three-year ceiling reflects this heightened betrayal.

sections.heading: Punishment for cheating by personation
sections.text: Whoever cheats by personation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Cheating by personation (Section 416) is punished more severely than ordinary cheating (one year under Section 417) because the impersonation adds a distinct layer of identity deception and may have wider social consequences.

sections.heading: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
sections.text: Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Cheating (as defined in Section 415)
Thereby dishonestly inducing the deceived person to:
(a) Deliver any property to any person; OR
(b) Make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security; OR
(c) Make, alter or destroy anything signed or sealed that is capable of being converted into a valuable security
sections.key_distinction_from_s417: Section 417 punishes mere cheating (one year). Section 420 is the aggravated form — where cheating results in actual delivery of property or manipulation of valuable securities — and carries a much higher punishment of up to seven years.
sections.key_principle: Section 420 is one of the most commonly invoked penal provisions in commercial fraud and white-collar crime in India. The 'valuable security' limb covers instruments like cheques, promissory notes, and deeds.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Against Property
chapters.sub_heading: Of Fraudulent Deeds and Dispositions of Property

sections.heading: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly or fraudulently removes, conceals or delivers to any person, or transfers or causes to be transferred to any person, without adequate consideration, any property, intending thereby to prevent, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby prevent, the distribution of that property according to law among his creditors or the creditors of any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Dishonest or fraudulent removal, concealment, delivery, or transfer of property
Without adequate consideration
Intent to prevent, or knowledge of likelihood of preventing, lawful distribution among creditors

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to prevent distribution of property among creditors
Knowledge that the removal or transfer is likely to prevent such distribution

sections.key_principle: Targets fraudulent insolvency — the deliberate dissipation or concealment of assets to defeat creditors' claims. Transfer must be without adequate consideration to attract this section.

sections.heading: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly or fraudulently prevents any debt or demand due to himself or to any other person from being made available according to law for payment of his debts or the debts of such other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Prevention of a debt or demand due to oneself or another person
From being made available for payment of debts according to law
Done dishonestly or fraudulently

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest or fraudulent intent to prevent a debt or demand from being applied toward payment of debts

sections.key_principle: Complements Section 421 by targeting the concealment or suppression of receivable debts (as opposed to removal of tangible property). Covers situations where a debtor fraudulently waives or withholds debts owed to him so as to keep those sums out of reach of his own creditors.

sections.heading: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly or fraudulently signs, executes or becomes a party to any deed or instrument which purports to transfer or subject to any charge any property, or any interest therein, and which contains any false statement relating to the consideration for such transfer or charge, or relating to the person or persons for whose use or benefit it is really intended to operate, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Signing, executing, or becoming a party to a deed or instrument
Deed purports to transfer property or subject it to a charge
Deed contains a false statement as to the consideration OR as to the person(s) for whose benefit it is intended
Done dishonestly or fraudulently

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest or fraudulent intent in executing a deed that contains a false statement of consideration or beneficial interest

sections.key_principle: Targets fraudulent deed execution in property transactions where the deed contains a false recital of consideration or conceals the true beneficiary. Critical in land-fraud cases, often charged alongside Sections 420 and 467.

sections.heading: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly or fraudulently conceals or removes any property of himself or any other person, or dishonestly or fraudulently assists in the concealment or removal thereof, or dishonestly releases any demand or claim to which he is entitled, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Dishonest or fraudulent concealment or removal of property (own or another person's); OR
Dishonest or fraudulent assistance in such concealment or removal; OR
Dishonest release of a demand or claim to which the person is entitled

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest or fraudulent intent to conceal, remove, or assist in concealing/removing property, or to release a claim

sections.key_principle: Broader than Section 421 — applies to concealment or removal of any property (not limited to creditor-fraud context) and also covers the dishonest release of a legally enforceable claim or demand. Often charged alongside Section 420 in property fraud cases.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Against Property

sections.heading: Mischief
sections.text: Whoever with intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to the public or to any person, causes the destruction of any property, or any such change in any property or in the situation thereof as destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or affects it injuriously, commits "mischief".
ingredients: Intent to cause or knowledge of likelihood of causing wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person
Causing destruction of property; OR
Causing any change in property or its situation that destroys or diminishes its value or utility, or injuriously affects it

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person
Knowledge that the act is likely to cause wrongful loss or damage to the public or any person

sections.key_principle: Mischief does not require the offender to intend loss specifically to the owner of the property; damage to any person by injury to any property suffices. Even property jointly owned by the offender may be the subject of mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A voluntarily burns a valuable security belonging to Z intending to cause wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Intentional burning of another's property with intent to cause wrongful loss constitutes mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A introduces water into an ice-house belonging to Z and thus causes the ice to melt, intending wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Any act causing diminution in the value or utility of property, done with intent to cause wrongful loss, is mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A voluntarily throws into a river a ring belonging to Z, with the intention of thereby causing wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Destruction or disposal of another's property with intent to cause wrongful loss is mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A, knowing that his effects are about to be taken in execution in order to satisfy a debt due from him to Z, destroys those effects, with the intention of thereby preventing Z from obtaining satisfaction of the debt, and of thus causing damage to Z. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Destruction of one's own property to frustrate a creditor's right of execution constitutes mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A having insured a ship, voluntarily causes the same to be cast away, with the intention of causing damage to the underwriters. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Deliberate destruction of insured property to defraud underwriters constitutes mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f)
illustrations.text: A causes a ship to be cast away, intending thereby to cause damage to Z who has lent money on bottomry on the ship. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Intentional destruction of property pledged as security, with intent to cause damage to the creditor, constitutes mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (g)
illustrations.text: A, having joint property with Z in a horse, shoots the horse, intending thereby to cause wrongful loss to Z. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Destruction of jointly owned property with intent to cause wrongful loss to the co-owner constitutes mischief.

illustrations.label: Illustration (h)
illustrations.text: A causes cattle to enter upon a field belonging to Z, intending to cause and knowing that he is likely to cause damage to Z's crop. A has committed mischief.
illustrations.key_principle: Causing cattle to damage another's crops with knowledge of likely damage constitutes mischief.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: It is not essential to the offence of mischief that the offender should intend to cause loss or damage to the owner of the property injured or destroyed. It is sufficient if he intends to cause, or knows that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage to any person by injuring any property, whether it belongs to that person or not.
explanations.plain_language: The victim of the wrongful loss need not be the owner of the damaged property. Causing loss to any person through property damage suffices.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: Mischief may be committed by an act affecting property belonging to the person who commits the act, or to that person and others jointly.
explanations.plain_language: One can commit mischief even against one's own property or jointly held property, provided the requisite intent to cause wrongful loss to another is present.

sections.heading: Punishment for mischief
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief as defined under Section 425
sections.key_principle: General punishment provision for simple mischief. Aggravated forms (Sections 427–440) attract higher punishment based on value of damage, type of property, or manner of commission.

sections.heading: Mischief causing damage to the amount of fifty rupees
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief and thereby causes loss or damage to the amount of fifty rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief (Section 425)
Loss or damage caused amounts to fifty rupees or more
sections.key_principle: Aggravated mischief based on quantum of damage — the threshold of fifty rupees triggers the higher punishment of up to two years as opposed to three months under Section 426.

sections.heading: Mischief by killing or maiming animal of the value of ten rupees
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming or rendering useless any animal or animals of the value of ten rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless any animal or animals
The animal(s) must be of a value of ten rupees or more
sections.key_principle: Special provision for mischief involving harm to animals. Value threshold of ten rupees applies. Section 429 covers specific high-value animals regardless of value.

sections.heading: Mischief by killing or maiming cattle, etc., of any value or any animal of the value of fifty rupees
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming or rendering useless, any elephant, camel, horse, mule, buffalo, bull, cow or ox, whatever may be the value thereof, or any other animal of the value of fifty rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless
Any elephant, camel, horse, mule, buffalo, bull, cow or ox (regardless of value); OR
Any other animal of the value of fifty rupees or more
sections.key_principle: Higher-punishment provision for mischief to agriculturally and commercially important animals regardless of value, or other animals worth fifty rupees or more. Cow slaughter attracts this section regardless of value.

sections.heading: Mischief by injury to works of irrigation or by wrongfully diverting water
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by doing any act which causes, or which he knows to be likely to cause, a diminution of the supply of water for agricultural purposes, or for food or drink for human beings or for animals which are property, or for cleanliness or for carrying on any manufacture, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by any act
The act causes or is known to be likely to cause diminution of water supply
Diminution affects: agricultural purposes; food/drink for humans or animals; cleanliness; or any manufacture

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause wrongful loss or damage through reduction of water supply
Knowledge that the act is likely to cause such diminution in water supply

sections.key_principle: Protects irrigation infrastructure and public water supply. The provision is broad, covering any reduction in supply of water for agriculture, human consumption, animal use, sanitation, or manufacturing.

sections.heading: Mischief by injury to public road, bridge, river or channel
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by doing any act which renders or which he knows to be likely to render any public road, bridge, navigable river or navigable channel, natural or artificial, impassable or less safe for travelling or conveying property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by any act
The act renders or is likely to render a public road, bridge, navigable river, or navigable channel (natural or artificial) impassable or less safe for travel or conveyance of property
sections.key_principle: Protects public transport infrastructure. Both natural and artificial waterways, as well as roads and bridges, are covered. The harm need only make the route 'less safe' — impassability is not required.

sections.heading: Mischief by causing inundation or obstruction to public drainage attended with damage
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by doing any act which causes or which he knows to be likely to cause an inundation or an obstruction to any public drainage attended with injury or damage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by any act
The act causes or is likely to cause inundation OR obstruction of public drainage
Such inundation or obstruction is attended with injury or damage
sections.key_principle: Covers deliberate tampering with public drainage systems leading to flooding or overflow damage. The resultant injury or damage is a necessary element.

sections.heading: Mischief by destroying, moving or rendering less useful a light-house or sea-mark
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by destroying or moving any light-house or other light used as a sea-mark, or any sea-mark or buoy or other thing placed as a guide for navigators, or by any act which renders any such light-house, sea-mark, buoy or other such thing as aforesaid less useful as a guide for navigators, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by destroying, moving, or tampering with a light-house, sea-mark, buoy, or other navigational aid
The act destroys, moves, or renders such aid less useful as a guide for navigators
sections.key_principle: Protects maritime safety infrastructure. Tampering with navigational aids endangers ships and lives at sea, justifying the elevated punishment of up to seven years.

sections.heading: Mischief by destroying or moving, etc., a land-mark fixed by public authority
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by destroying or moving any land-mark fixed by the authority of a public servant, or by any act which renders such land-mark less useful as such, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by destroying or moving a land-mark fixed by a public servant's authority
OR by any act which renders such land-mark less useful
sections.key_principle: Protects official boundary and survey marks from tampering. The land-mark must have been fixed under public authority for this section to apply.

sections.heading: Mischief by fire or explosive substance with intent to cause damage to amount of one hundred or (in case of agricultural produce) ten rupees
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by fire or any explosive substance intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, damage to any property to the amount of one hundred rupees or upwards or (where the property is agricultural produce) ten rupees or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by fire or any explosive substance
Intent or knowledge that the act will cause damage to property worth one hundred rupees or more (or ten rupees or more in case of agricultural produce)

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause damage of the specified amount by fire or explosive
Knowledge that such damage is likely to be caused

sections.key_principle: Enhanced punishment for mischief by fire or explosives. Special protection for agricultural produce with a lower threshold (ten rupees), reflecting the vulnerability and importance of crops.

footnotes.text: Words "or (where the property is agricultural produce) ten rupees or upwards" inserted by Act 8 of 1882, s. 10.

sections.heading: Mischief by fire or explosive substance with intent to destroy house, etc.
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief by fire or any explosive substance, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, the destruction of any building which is ordinarily used as a place of worship or as a human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of mischief by fire or any explosive substance
Intent or knowledge that destruction will be caused to a building
The building is ordinarily used as a place of worship, human dwelling, or place for the custody of property

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to destroy such a building by fire or explosive
Knowledge that destruction of such a building is likely

sections.key_principle: Most severe mischief provision — covers arson of dwellings, places of worship, or property storage buildings. Imprisonment for life is an option given the potential for mass harm and loss of shelter or sacred spaces.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief to any decked vessel or any vessel of a burden of twenty tons or upwards, intending to destroy or render unsafe, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby destroy or render unsafe, that vessel, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of mischief to a decked vessel or a vessel of twenty tons burden or more
Intent to destroy or render the vessel unsafe; OR
Knowledge that the act is likely to destroy or render the vessel unsafe
sections.key_principle: Protects vessels of significant size from deliberate sabotage. A decked vessel or any vessel of twenty tons or more qualifies. See Section 438 for aggravated form using fire or explosives.

sections.heading: Punishment for the mischief described in section 437 committed by fire or explosive substance
sections.text: Whoever commits, or attempts to commit, by fire or any explosive substance, such mischief as is described in the last preceding section, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission or attempt to commit mischief described under Section 437
Done by means of fire or any explosive substance
sections.key_principle: Aggravated form of Section 437 where fire or explosives are used to destroy or render unsafe a qualifying vessel. Notably, even an attempt is punishable under this provision, unlike the base offence under Section 437.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.
sections.text: Whoever intentionally runs any vessel aground or ashore, intending to commit theft of any property contained therein or to dishonestly misappropriate any such property, or with intent that such theft or misappropriation of property may be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Intentionally running a vessel aground or ashore
With intent to commit theft of property in the vessel; OR
With intent to dishonestly misappropriate such property; OR
With intent that such theft or misappropriation be committed by another

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit or facilitate theft or dishonest misappropriation of property in the grounded vessel

sections.key_principle: Covers deliberate wrecking of a vessel to loot its cargo. Unlike Sections 437–438 which focus on destruction, this provision targets running aground as a prelude to theft or misappropriation.

sections.heading: Mischief committed after preparation made for causing death or hurt
sections.text: Whoever commits mischief, having made preparation for causing to any person death, or hurt, or wrongful restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of mischief (Section 425)
Prior preparation made to cause death, hurt, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof to any person
sections.key_principle: Aggravated mischief where preparation to cause violence or restraint preceded the act. The combination of mischief with violent preparation attracts higher punishment reflecting the greater danger posed by the offender.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Against Property

sections.heading: Criminal trespass
sections.text: Whoever enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property, or having lawfully entered into or upon such property, unlawfully remains there with intent thereby to intimidate, insult or annoy any such person, or with intent to commit an offence, is said to commit "criminal trespass".
ingredients: Entry into or upon property in another's possession; OR
Remaining unlawfully in property after lawful entry
With intent to: commit an offence; OR intimidate, insult, or annoy any person in possession

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit an offence upon entry or while remaining
Intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person in possession

sections.key_principle: Criminal trespass is ordinary trespass plus a specific unlawful intent. Mere entry without such intent is not criminal trespass. Unlawful remaining after lawful entry with the requisite intent also qualifies.

sections.heading: House-trespass
sections.text: Whoever commits criminal trespass by entering into or remaining in any building, tent or vessel used as a human dwelling or any building used as a place for worship, or as a place for the custody of property, is said to commit "house-trespass".
ingredients: Commission of criminal trespass (Section 441)
By entering into or remaining in a building, tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling; OR
A building used as a place of worship; OR
A building used as a place for the custody of property
sections.key_principle: House-trespass is a specific and aggravated form of criminal trespass involving entry into or remaining in a dwelling, place of worship, or property storage structure. Even introduction of a part of the body is sufficient — see Explanation.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: The introduction of any part of the criminal trespasser's body is entering sufficient to constitute house-trespass.
explanations.plain_language: Partial bodily entry (e.g., inserting a hand through a window or opening) is sufficient to constitute house-trespass; complete physical entry is not required.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass having taken precautions to conceal such house-trespass from some person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser from the building, tent or vessel which is the subject of the trespass, is said to commit "lurking house-trespass".
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)
Having taken precautions to conceal the trespass from a person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser
sections.key_principle: Lurking house-trespass is house-trespass with stealth. The precautionary concealment from an authorised person distinguishes it from simple house-trespass and attracts higher punishment under Section 453.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass by night
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass after sunset and before sunrise, is said to commit "lurking house-trespass by night".
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass (Section 443)
Committed after sunset and before sunrise
sections.key_principle: Nighttime lurking house-trespass is the most aggravated definitional form before house-breaking. The nocturnal element is treated as a further aggravating factor, attracting enhanced punishment under Section 456.

sections.heading: House-breaking
sections.text: A person is said to commit "house-breaking" who commits house-trespass if he effects his entrance into the house or any part of it in any of the six ways hereinafter described; or if, being in the house or any part of it for the purpose of committing an offence, or having committed an offence therein, he quits the house or any part of it in any of such six ways, that is to say: First — If he enters or quits through a passage made by himself, or by any abettor of the house-trespass, in order to the committing of the house-trespass. Secondly — If he enters or quits through any passage not intended by any person, other than himself or an abettor of the offence, for human entrance; or through any passage to which he has obtained access by scaling or climbing over any wall or building. Thirdly — If he enters or quits through any passage which he or any abettor of the house-trespass has opened, in order to the committing of the house-trespass by any means by which that passage was not intended by the occupier of the house to be opened. Fourthly — If he enters or quits by opening any lock in order to the committing of the house-trespass, or in order to the quitting of the house after a house-trespass. Fifthly — If he effects his entrance or departure by using criminal force or committing an assault, or by threatening any person with assault. Sixthly — If he enters or quits by any passage which he knows to have been fastened against such entrance or departure, and to have been unfastened by himself or by an abettor of the house-trespass.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)

Entry or exit effected through one of six specified modes: (1) passage made by offender/abettor; (2) unintended passage or by scaling; (3) passage opened by offender/abettor by unauthorised means; (4) by opening any lock; (5) by criminal force, assault, or threat thereof; (6) through a passage known to be fastened and unfastened by offender/abettor
sections.key_principle: House-breaking is house-trespass where entry or exit is gained by force, stealth, or circumvention of security measures. Importantly, unlawful exit after a completed offence by one of the six modes also qualifies. An out-house with immediate internal communication to the main house is treated as part of the house.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A commits house-trespass by making a hole through the wall of Z's house, and putting his hand through the aperture. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under First mode — passage made by offender
illustrations.key_principle: Creating a hole in a wall to gain entry is house-breaking even if the entry is partial.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A commits house-trespass by creeping into a ship at a port-hole between decks. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Second mode — passage not intended for human entrance
illustrations.key_principle: Using an opening not intended for human entry (such as a port-hole) constitutes house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A commits house-trespass by entering Z's house through a window. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.key_principle: Entry through a window, which is not intended as a human entrance, is house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d)
illustrations.text: A commits house-trespass by entering Z's house through the door, having opened a door which was fastened. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Sixth mode — fastened passage unfastened by offender
illustrations.key_principle: Opening a fastened door to gain entry is house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (e)
illustrations.text: A commits house-trespass by entering Z's house through the door, having lifted a latch by putting a wire through a hole in the door. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Third mode — passage opened by unauthorised means
illustrations.key_principle: Using an implement to open a door by means not intended by the occupier constitutes house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (f)
illustrations.text: A finds the key of Z's house door, which Z had lost, and commits house-trespass by entering Z's house, having opened the door with that key. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Fourth mode — entry by opening a lock
illustrations.key_principle: Using a found key without authorisation to open a lock and gain entry is house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (g)
illustrations.text: Z is standing in his doorway. A forces a passage by knocking Z down, and commits house-trespass by entering the house. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Fifth mode — entry by criminal force or assault
illustrations.key_principle: Physically removing a person blocking entry through force in order to enter constitutes house-breaking.

illustrations.label: Illustration (h)
illustrations.text: Z, the door-keeper of Y, is standing in Y's doorway. A commits house-trespass by entering the house, having deterred Z from opposing him by threatening to beat him. This is house-breaking.
illustrations.verdict: House-breaking under Fifth mode — entry by threat of assault
illustrations.key_principle: Threatening a person guarding entry to gain access constitutes house-breaking.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: Any out-house or building occupied with a house, and between which and such house there is an immediate internal communication, is part of the house within the meaning of this section.
explanations.plain_language: An attached outhouse, garage, or outbuilding with direct internal access to the main dwelling is treated as part of the house for the purpose of this section.

sections.heading: House-breaking by night
sections.text: Whoever commits house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise, is said to commit "house-breaking by night".
ingredients: Commission of house-breaking (Section 445)
Committed after sunset and before sunrise
sections.key_principle: House-breaking by night is the most aggravated form of house-breaking, attracting punishment under Sections 456–460. The nocturnal element significantly increases the danger posed to occupants.

sections.heading: Punishment for criminal trespass
sections.text: Whoever commits criminal trespass shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of criminal trespass as defined under Section 441
sections.key_principle: General punishment for simple criminal trespass. Aggravated forms (house-trespass, lurking house-trespass, house-breaking) attract significantly higher punishment under subsequent sections.

sections.heading: Punishment for house-trespass
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass as defined under Section 442
sections.key_principle: Punishment for simple house-trespass. Sections 449–455 provide aggravated punishment where house-trespass is accompanied by a more serious intended offence, preparation for violence, or nocturnal commission.

sections.heading: House-trespass in order to commit offence punishable with death
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass in order to the committing of any offence punishable with death, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)
With intent to commit an offence punishable with death

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit a capital offence during or as part of the house-trespass

sections.key_principle: Most severe house-trespass provision, tracking the gravity of the intended offence. Where the intended offence is capital (e.g., murder), the house-trespass itself warrants up to life imprisonment. Note: only rigorous (not simple) imprisonment is prescribed as the lesser alternative.
