footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: House-trespass in order to commit offence punishable with imprisonment for life
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass in order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment for life, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)
With intent to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment for life

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit an offence carrying life imprisonment during or as part of the house-trespass

sections.key_principle: Second-tier aggravated house-trespass provision, applying where the intended offence carries imprisonment for life (e.g., dacoity, certain forms of grievous hurt). Punishment follows the intended offence's gravity but is capped at ten years imprisonment of either description.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Against Property

sections.heading: House-trespass in order to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass in order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if the offence intended to be committed is theft, the term of the imprisonment may be extended to seven years.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)
With intent to commit any offence punishable with imprisonment

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment during or as part of the house-trespass

punishment_options.condition: Up to two years (general); up to seven years if intended offence is theft

sections.key_principle: Third-tier aggravated house-trespass provision. Where the intended offence carries imprisonment (but not death or life imprisonment), the basic term is two years; theft as the intended offence elevates the cap to seven years, reflecting the frequency of house-trespass to commit theft.

sections.heading: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint
sections.text: Whoever commits house-trespass, having made preparation for causing hurt to any person or for assaulting any person, or for wrongfully restraining any person, or for putting any person in fear of hurt, or of assault, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of house-trespass (Section 442)
Having made preparation for causing hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof to any person

mens_rea_modes.description: Preparatory intent to cause hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof, combined with the commission of house-trespass

sections.key_principle: Aggravated house-trespass based on violent preparation. Prior preparation — such as carrying a weapon or binding material — for inflicting hurt, assault, or unlawful restraint elevates the offence significantly above simple house-trespass.

sections.heading: Punishment for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass or house-breaking, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass (Section 443); OR
Commission of house-breaking (Section 445)
sections.key_principle: General punishment for lurking house-trespass and house-breaking — both forms involve stealth or forcible/unauthorised entry, justifying higher punishment than simple house-trespass (Section 448). Sections 454–460 deal with aggravated variants.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking in order to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass or house-breaking, in order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if the offence intended to be committed is theft, the term of the imprisonment may be extended to ten years.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass (Section 443) or house-breaking (Section 445)
With intent to commit any offence punishable with imprisonment

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment during or following the lurking house-trespass or house-breaking

punishment_options.condition: Up to three years (general); up to ten years if intended offence is theft

sections.key_principle: Aggravated form combining stealth/forcible entry with intent to commit an imprisonable offence. The theft-specific enhancement to ten years reflects that lurking house-trespass or house-breaking to steal is a common and serious pattern of offending.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass, or house-breaking, having made preparation for causing hurt to any person, or for assaulting any person, or for wrongfully restraining any person, or for putting any person in fear of hurt or of assault or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass (Section 443) or house-breaking (Section 445)
Having made preparation for causing hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof to any person

mens_rea_modes.description: Preparatory intent to cause hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof, combined with lurking house-trespass or house-breaking

sections.key_principle: Serious aggravated form — lurking or house-breaking compounded by preparedness to commit violence. The combination of stealth/forced entry and violent preparation justifies the substantially elevated ceiling of ten years.

sections.heading: Punishment for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass by night, or house-breaking by night, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass by night (Section 444); OR
Commission of house-breaking by night (Section 446)
sections.key_principle: The addition of the nocturnal element to lurking house-trespass or house-breaking adds one year to the general cap compared to Section 453. Sections 457–460 cover yet more serious nighttime variants.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night in order to commit offence punishable with imprisonment
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass by night, or house-breaking by night, in order to the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the offence intended to be committed is theft, the term of the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass by night (Section 444) or house-breaking by night (Section 446)
With intent to commit any offence punishable with imprisonment

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment during or following the nocturnal lurking house-trespass or house-breaking

punishment_options.condition: Up to five years (general); up to fourteen years if intended offence is theft

sections.key_principle: One of the most commonly charged house-breaking provisions. Nocturnal house-breaking with intent to steal carries up to fourteen years, reflecting the danger such offences pose to occupants. The night element dramatically elevates the punishment compared to the daytime equivalent under Section 454.

sections.heading: Lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night after preparation for hurt, assault, or wrongful restraint
sections.text: Whoever commits lurking house-trespass by night, or house-breaking by night, having made preparation for causing hurt to any person or for assaulting any person, or for wrongfully restraining any person, or for putting any person in fear of hurt, or of assault, or of wrongful restraint, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to fourteen years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass by night (Section 444) or house-breaking by night (Section 446)
Having made preparation for causing hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof to any person

mens_rea_modes.description: Preparatory intent to cause hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or fear thereof, combined with nocturnal lurking house-trespass or house-breaking

sections.key_principle: The most severe non-life-imprisonment house-trespass provision not involving actual harm. Combines stealth/forced nocturnal entry with prior preparation for violence — just short of Sections 459–460 which require actual grievous hurt or death.

sections.heading: Grievous hurt caused whilst committing lurking house-trespass or house-breaking
sections.text: Whoever, whilst committing lurking house-trespass or house-breaking, causes grievous hurt to any person or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass (Section 443) or house-breaking (Section 445)
While so committing, causes grievous hurt to any person; OR
Attempts to cause death or grievous hurt to any person

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention or knowledge resulting in grievous hurt or attempt to cause death or grievous hurt during the commission of lurking house-trespass or house-breaking

sections.key_principle: Provides for life imprisonment where grievous hurt is actually caused or death/grievous hurt is attempted during lurking house-trespass or house-breaking. The transition from preparation (Section 458) to actual harm triggers the life imprisonment option.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: All persons jointly concerned in lurking house-trespass or house-breaking by night punishable where death or grievous hurt caused by one of them
sections.text: If, at the time of the committing of lurking house-trespass by night or house-breaking by night, any person guilty of such offence shall voluntarily cause or attempt to cause death or grievous hurt to any person, every person jointly concerned in committing such lurking house-trespass by night or house-breaking by night, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of lurking house-trespass by night or house-breaking by night
At the time of the offence, any one of the persons guilty thereof voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt to any person
Every person jointly concerned in the offence is equally liable

mens_rea_modes.description: Joint participation in nocturnal lurking house-trespass or house-breaking; one participant's voluntary act of causing or attempting death or grievous hurt renders all jointly liable

punishment_options.condition: Maximum sentence applicable to all jointly concerned persons

sections.key_principle: Embodies the principle of joint liability — all participants in nocturnal lurking house-trespass or house-breaking share the enhanced punishment when any one of them voluntarily causes or attempts death or grievous hurt, regardless of individual participation in that specific act of violence. Applies exclusively to nighttime offences.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property
sections.text: Whoever dishonestly or with intent to commit mischief, breaks open or unfastens any closed receptacle which contains or which he believes to contain property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Breaking open or unfastening any closed receptacle
The receptacle contains or is believed by the offender to contain property
Done dishonestly or with intent to commit mischief

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest intent — intent to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss
Intent to commit mischief (Section 425)

sections.key_principle: Covers dishonest or mischievous breaking of any closed receptacle — boxes, trunks, safes, etc. — believed to contain property. The offender's belief that the receptacle contains property is sufficient; actual contents are irrelevant to liability.

sections.heading: Punishment for same offence when committed by person entrusted with custody
sections.text: Whoever, being entrusted with any closed receptacle which contains or which he believes to contain property, without having authority to open the same, dishonestly, or with intent to commit mischief, breaks open or unfastens that receptacle, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Being entrusted with a closed receptacle which contains or is believed to contain property
Without authority to open it
Dishonestly or with intent to commit mischief, breaking open or unfastening it

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest intent by a person entrusted with custody of the receptacle
Intent to commit mischief by such a person

sections.key_principle: Aggravated form of Section 461 — breach of trust by a custodian warrants an additional year of imprisonment. The entrustment creates a fiduciary obligation, and dishonest violation of that obligation is treated more seriously than a stranger's identical act.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Relating to Documents and to Property Marks

sections.heading: Forgery
sections.text: Whoever makes any false document or false electronic record or part of a document or electronic record, with intent to cause damage or injury, to the public or to any person, or to support any claim or title, or to cause any person to part with property, or to enter into any express or implied contract, or with intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed, commits forgery.
ingredients: Making any false document or false electronic record, or part thereof

With intent to: cause damage or injury to the public or any person; OR support any claim or title; OR cause any person to part with property; OR cause any person to enter into any express or implied contract; OR commit fraud or enable fraud to be committed

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person
Intent to support a false claim or title
Intent to cause any person to part with property
Intent to cause any person to enter into an express or implied contract
Intent to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed

sections.key_principle: Foundational definition of forgery. Extends to electronic records by virtue of the IT Act amendments. Making a false document with any of the five specified intents constitutes forgery — the intents are disjunctive. See Section 464 for what constitutes 'making a false document'.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Making a false document
sections.text: A person is said to make a false document or false electronic record — First: Who dishonestly or fraudulently makes, signs, seals or executes a document or part of a document, or makes or transmits any electronic record, or affixes any electronic signature on any electronic record, or makes any mark denoting the execution of a document or the authenticity of the electronic signature, with the intention of causing it to be believed that such document, electronic record or electronic signature was made, signed, sealed, executed, transmitted or affixed by or by the authority of a person by whom or by whose authority he knows that it was not made, signed, sealed, executed or affixed; or Secondly: Who without lawful authority, dishonestly or fraudulently, by cancellation or otherwise, alters a document or an electronic record in any material part thereof, after it has been made, executed or affixed with electronic signature either by himself or by any other person, whether such person be living or dead at the time of such alteration; or Thirdly: Who dishonestly or fraudulently causes any person to sign, seal, execute or alter a document or an electronic record or to affix his electronic signature on any electronic record knowing that such person by reason of unsoundness of mind or intoxication cannot, or that by reason of deception practised upon him, he does not know the contents of the document or electronic record or the nature of the alteration.
ingredients: First mode: Dishonestly or fraudulently making, signing, sealing, executing, transmitting a document/electronic record, or affixing an electronic signature, with intent to cause it to be believed it was done by or under authority of a person who did not do so
Second mode: Without lawful authority, dishonestly or fraudulently altering a document or electronic record in any material part after it has been made or executed

Third mode: Dishonestly or fraudulently causing another person (who due to unsoundness of mind, intoxication, or deception does not know the contents or nature of the alteration) to sign, seal, execute, alter a document or electronic record or affix an electronic signature

mens_rea_modes.description: Dishonest or fraudulent intent in all three modes of making a false document

sections.key_principle: Defines three modes of making a false document: (1) fabrication by impersonation or false authority; (2) material alteration without authority; (3) procuring execution by a person incapable of understanding the document due to mental incapacity, intoxication, or deception. Extends fully to electronic records and electronic signatures. A person may forge using their own name if the intent is to deceive as to the identity of the signatory.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a) — Main
illustrations.text: A has a letter of credit upon B for rupees 10,000, written by Z. A, in order to defraud B, adds a cipher to the 10,000, and makes the sum 1,00,000 intending that it may be believed by B that Z so wrote the letter. A has committed forgery.
illustrations.key_principle: Material alteration of a document to inflate a stated amount constitutes forgery under the Second mode.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b) — Main
illustrations.text: A, without Z's authority, affixes Z's seal to a document purporting to be a conveyance of an estate from Z to A, with the intention of selling the estate to B and thereby obtaining from B the purchase-money. A has committed forgery.
illustrations.key_principle: Affixing another's seal without authority to falsely authenticate a document constitutes forgery under the First mode.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c) — Main
illustrations.text: A picks up a cheque on a banker signed by B, payable to bearer, but without any sum having been inserted in the cheque. A fraudulently fills up the cheque by inserting the sum of ten thousand rupees. A commits forgery.
illustrations.key_principle: Filling in an incomplete document in a manner not authorised by the signatory constitutes forgery.

illustrations.label: Illustration (d) — Main
illustrations.text: A leaves with B, his agent, a cheque signed by A, without inserting the sum payable and authorizes B to fill up the cheque by inserting a sum not exceeding ten thousand rupees. B fraudulently fills up the cheque by inserting the sum of twenty thousand rupees. B commits forgery.
illustrations.key_principle: Exceeding the authority conferred to fill in a document, with fraudulent intent, constitutes forgery even where the agent was authorised to complete the document to a lesser extent.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a) — Explanation 1
illustrations.text: A signs his own name to a bill of exchange, intending that it may be believed that the bill was drawn by another person of the same name. A has committed forgery.
illustrations.key_principle: Signing one's own name with intent to impersonate another person of the same name constitutes forgery — the false document need not bear a false name.

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: A man's signature of his own name may amount to forgery.
explanations.plain_language: Using one's own genuine signature can still constitute forgery if the intent is to create a false belief that the document was executed by a different person of the same name.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: The making of a false document in the name of a fictitious person, intending it to be believed that the document was made by a real person, or in the name of a deceased person, intending it to be believed that the document was made by the person in his lifetime, may amount to forgery.
explanations.plain_language: Creating a document in the name of a fictitious or deceased person, to be passed off as genuine, may constitute forgery.

explanations.label: Explanation 3
explanations.text: For the purposes of this section, the expression 'affixing electronic signature' shall have the meaning assigned to it in clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).
explanations.plain_language: The term 'affixing electronic signature' has the specific meaning given to it under the Information Technology Act, 2000.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).
Subs. by Act 10 of 2009, s. 51, for "digital signature" (w.e.f. 27-10-2009).

sections.heading: Punishment for forgery
sections.text: Whoever commits forgery shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Commission of forgery as defined under Sections 463 and 464
sections.key_principle: General punishment for simple forgery. Sections 466–469 provide enhanced punishment where the forgery involves specific high-value instruments (court records, wills, valuable securities) or is committed with specific aggravated intent (cheating, harming reputation).

sections.heading: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.
sections.text: Whoever forges a document or an electronic record, purporting to be a record or proceeding of or in a Court of Justice, or a register of birth, baptism, marriage or burial, or a register kept by a public servant as such, or a certificate or document purporting to be made by a public servant in his official capacity, or an authority to institute or defend a suit, or to take any proceedings therein, or to confess judgment, or a power of attorney, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of forgery (Sections 463–464)

The forged document or electronic record purports to be: a court record or proceeding; a register of birth, baptism, marriage, or burial; a register kept by a public servant; a certificate or document made by a public servant in official capacity; an authority to institute or defend a suit or take proceedings; a confession of judgment; or a power of attorney
sections.key_principle: Elevated punishment for forgery of official and quasi-official documents — court records, public registers, and official certificates — reflecting the serious harm caused by undermining public confidence in state records and judicial processes. The explanation extends 'register' to electronic records under the IT Act, 2000.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: For the purposes of this section, 'register' includes any list, data or record of any entries maintained in the electronic form as defined in clause (r) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).
explanations.plain_language: The word 'register' encompasses electronic records and databases maintained by public authorities, not merely physical registers.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.
sections.text: Whoever forges a document which purports to be a valuable security or a will, or an authority to adopt a son, or which purports to give authority to any person to make or transfer any valuable security, or to receive the principal, interest or dividends thereon, or to receive or deliver any money, movable property, or valuable security, or any document purporting to be an acquittance or receipt acknowledging the payment of money, or an acquittance or receipt for the delivery of any movable property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of forgery (Sections 463–464)

The forged document purports to be: a valuable security; a will; an authority to adopt a son; an authority to make or transfer a valuable security; an authority to receive principal, interest, or dividends; an authority to receive or deliver money, movable property, or a valuable security; an acquittance or receipt for money; or an acquittance or receipt for delivery of movable property or a valuable security
sections.key_principle: Most severe forgery provision — reserved for forgery of instruments with the highest potential for financial and proprietary harm: wills, negotiable instruments, securities, and receipts. Life imprisonment is available. Section 467 documents are the reference point for aggravated punishment in Sections 472–475.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Forgery for purpose of cheating
sections.text: Whoever commits forgery, intending that the document or electronic record forged shall be used for the purpose of cheating, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of forgery (Sections 463–464)
With intent that the forged document or electronic record shall be used for the purpose of cheating

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent that the forged instrument be used to cheat any person

sections.key_principle: Aggravated forgery based on purpose: where the forged document or electronic record is intended to be deployed in a cheating scheme, the punishment escalates from two years (Section 465) to seven years. Frequently charged alongside Section 420 in fraud cases.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Forgery for purpose of harming reputation
sections.text: Whoever commits forgery, intending that the document or electronic record forged shall harm the reputation of any party, or knowing that it is likely to be used for that purpose, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commission of forgery (Sections 463–464)
With intent that the forged document or electronic record shall harm the reputation of any party; OR
With knowledge that it is likely to be used for that purpose

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent that the forged document harm the reputation of any person
Knowledge that the forged document is likely to be used to harm reputation

sections.key_principle: Forgery aimed at reputational harm as opposed to financial gain. The provision covers both intent and knowledge of likely reputational damage. Punishment is lower than Section 468 but higher than simple forgery under Section 465, reflecting the nature of the harm caused.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Forged document
sections.text: A false document or electronic record made wholly or in part by forgery is designated "a forged document or electronic record".
ingredients: A false document or electronic record
Made wholly or in part by forgery (as defined in Sections 463–464)
sections.key_principle: A definitional section that labels the product of forgery as a 'forged document or electronic record'. The document or record need only be partly forged — a genuine document with a materially forged portion qualifies in its entirety as forged. This definition is referenced by Section 471.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for "document" (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Using as genuine a forged document or electronic record
sections.text: Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document or electronic record which he knows or has reason to believe to be a forged document or electronic record, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had forged such document or electronic record.
ingredients: Using a document or electronic record as genuine
Done fraudulently or dishonestly
The person knows or has reason to believe the document or electronic record to be forged

mens_rea_modes.description: Fraudulent or dishonest use of a document the person knows or has reason to believe is forged

punishment_options.type: Same punishment as for forging the document
punishment_options.condition: User is punished as if they had forged the document or electronic record — so punishment tracks the applicable forgery section (465, 466, 467, 468, or 469)

sections.key_principle: Punishes the user of a forged document as severely as the forger. Knowledge or reason to believe the document is forged is the key element. Particularly significant because it catches downstream parties in forgery chains even where they did not themselves create the false document.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for "document" (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Making or possessing counterfeit seal, etc., with intent to commit forgery punishable under section 467
sections.text: Whoever makes or counterfeits any seal, plate or other instrument for making an impression, intending that the same shall be used for the purpose of committing any forgery which would be punishable under section 467 of this Code, or, with such intent, has in his possession any such seal, plate or other instrument, knowing the same to be counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Making or counterfeiting any seal, plate, or other instrument for making an impression; OR
Possessing such a counterfeit seal, plate, or instrument knowing it to be counterfeit
With intent to use it to commit forgery punishable under Section 467

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to use the counterfeit seal or instrument to commit forgery of a document covered by Section 467 (valuable securities, wills, etc.)

sections.key_principle: Targets the preparatory stage of high-value forgery — making or possessing tools designed to forge Section 467 documents. Life imprisonment reflects the seriousness of the intended target (valuable securities, wills). Mere possession with knowledge and intent suffices; actual forgery need not have occurred.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Making or possessing counterfeit seal, etc., with intent to commit forgery punishable otherwise
sections.text: Whoever makes or counterfeits any seal, plate or other instrument for making an impression, intending that the same shall be used for the purpose of committing any forgery which would be punishable under any section of this Chapter other than section 467, or, with such intent, has in his possession any such seal, plate or other instrument, knowing the same to be counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Making or counterfeiting any seal, plate, or other instrument for making an impression; OR
Possessing such a counterfeit seal, plate, or instrument knowing it to be counterfeit
With intent to use it to commit forgery punishable under any Chapter XVIII section other than Section 467

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent to use the counterfeit seal or instrument to commit forgery under any Chapter XVIII provision except Section 467

sections.key_principle: Counterpart to Section 472 for lesser-grade forgery tools — same act (making/possessing counterfeit seals or instruments) but intended for forgeries other than those in Section 467. Life imprisonment is not available here, distinguishing it from the higher-risk Section 472 category.

sections.heading: Having possession of document described in section 466 or 467, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine
sections.text: Whoever has in his possession any document or electronic record, knowing the same to be forged and intending that the same shall fraudulently or dishonestly be used as genuine, shall, if the document or electronic record is one of the description mentioned in section 466 of this Code, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if the document is one of the description mentioned in section 467, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description, for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Possession of a document or electronic record
Knowing it to be forged
Intending that it shall fraudulently or dishonestly be used as genuine
The document is of the description in Section 466 or Section 467

mens_rea_modes.description: Knowledge that the possessed document is forged, combined with intent to use it fraudulently or dishonestly as genuine

punishment_options.type: If Section 466 document: Imprisonment of either description
punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, also liable to fine

punishment_options.type: If Section 467 document: Imprisonment for life
punishment_options.condition: Maximum sentence, also liable to fine

punishment_options.type: If Section 467 document: Imprisonment of either description
punishment_options.condition: Up to seven years, also liable to fine

sections.key_principle: Possession offence targeting holders of forged Section 466 or 467 documents with intent to use them. Unlike Section 471 (which punishes actual use), this provision punishes mere possession with fraudulent intent. Life imprisonment is available for Section 467 documents.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).
Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Counterfeiting device or mark used for authenticating documents described in section 467, or possessing counterfeit marked material
sections.text: Whoever counterfeits upon, or in the substance of, any material, any device or mark used for the purpose of authenticating any document described in section 467 of this Code, intending that such device or mark shall be used for the purpose of giving the appearance of authenticity to any document then forged or thereafter to be forged on such material, or who, with such intent, has in his possession any material upon or in the substance of which any such device or mark has been counterfeited, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Counterfeiting upon or in any material any device or mark used to authenticate a Section 467 document; OR
Possessing material upon which such a device or mark has been counterfeited
With intent that such device or mark shall give apparent authenticity to forged documents on that material

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent that the counterfeited device or mark shall be used to lend apparent authenticity to forged Section 467 documents

sections.key_principle: Targets preparation to forge Section 467 documents at the authentication-mark level — counterfeiting the stamps, seals, or marks used to authenticate valuable securities, wills, etc. Life imprisonment underscores the gravity of enabling large-scale financial forgery.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Counterfeiting device or mark used for authenticating documents other than those described in section 467, or possessing counterfeit marked material
sections.text: Whoever counterfeits upon, or in the substance of, any material, any device or mark used for the purpose of authenticating any document or electronic record other than the documents described in section 467 of this Code, intending that such device or mark shall be used for the purpose of giving the appearance of authenticity to any document then forged or thereafter to be forged on such material, or who with such intent, has in his possession any material upon or in the substance of which any such device or mark has been counterfeited, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Counterfeiting upon or in any material any device or mark used to authenticate any document or electronic record other than a Section 467 document; OR
Possessing material upon which such a device or mark has been counterfeited
With intent to give apparent authenticity to forged documents on that material

mens_rea_modes.description: Intent that the counterfeited device or mark shall be used to give the appearance of authenticity to forged non-Section 467 documents or electronic records

sections.key_principle: Counterpart to Section 475 for documents other than those in Section 467. Extends expressly to electronic records. Life imprisonment is not available, distinguishing it from Section 475.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for "any document" (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

sections.heading: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security
sections.text: Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly, or with intent to cause damage or injury to the public or to any person, cancels, destroys or defaces, or attempts to cancel, destroy or deface, or secretes or attempts to secrete any document which is or purports to be a will, or an authority to adopt a son, or any valuable security, or commits mischief in respect of such document, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Fraudulently, dishonestly, or with intent to cause damage or injury
Cancelling, destroying, defacing, secreting, or attempting to do so, or committing mischief in respect of
Any document that is or purports to be a will, an authority to adopt a son, or any valuable security

mens_rea_modes.description: Fraudulent or dishonest intent
Intent to cause damage or injury to the public or any person

sections.key_principle: Suppression or destruction counterpart to Section 467 (which deals with fabrication). Punishes the deliberate elimination of wills, adoption authorities, or valuable securities with the same severity as forging them — life imprisonment is available. Even an attempt or secretion suffices.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for "transportation for life" (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Falsification of accounts
sections.text: Whoever, being a clerk, officer or servant, or employed or acting in the capacity of a clerk, officer or servant, wilfully, and with intent to defraud, destroys, alters, mutilates or falsifies any book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security or account which belongs to or is in the possession of his employer, or has been received by him for or on behalf of his employer, or wilfully, and with intent to defraud, makes or abets the making of any false entry in, or omits or alters or abets the omission or alteration of any material particular from or in, any such book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security or account, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: The offender is or acts as a clerk, officer, or servant
Wilfully and with intent to defraud

Destroys, alters, mutilates, or falsifies any book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security, or account belonging to or in the possession of the employer or received on the employer's behalf; OR
Makes or abets any false entry in such records; OR
Omits, alters, or abets the omission or alteration of any material particular in such records

mens_rea_modes.description: Wilful act combined with intent to defraud — both elements must coexist

sections.key_principle: Occupational fraud by employees — targets clerks, officers, and servants who falsify their employer's accounts or records. The section expressly covers abetment of false entries and omissions. Critically, a general intent to defraud is sufficient — no specific person need be named as the intended victim.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: It shall be sufficient in any charge under this section to allege a general intent to defraud without naming any particular person intended to be defrauded or specifying any particular sum of money intended to be the subject of the fraud, or any particular day on which the offence was committed.
explanations.plain_language: In charging this offence, it is not necessary to identify the specific victim, amount defrauded, or exact date — a general allegation of fraudulent intent suffices.

footnotes.text: Added by Act 3 of 1895, s. 4.
Subs. by Act 21 of 2000, s. 91 and the First Sch., for "book, paper, writing" (w.e.f. 17-10-2000).

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Relating to Documents and to Property Marks

sections.heading: Trade Mark
sections.text: [Trade Mark.] Repealed by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 (43 of 1958), s. 135 and Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).
sections.key_principle: Originally defined 'trade mark'. Repealed and superseded by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, and subsequently by the Trade Marks Act, 1999.

footnotes.text: Subs. by Act 4 of 1889, s. 3, for the original heading and ss. 478 to 489.

sections.heading: Property mark
sections.text: A mark used for denoting that movable property belongs to a particular person is called a property mark.
ingredients: A mark
Used for denoting that movable property belongs to a particular person
sections.key_principle: Defines 'property mark' as any mark used to identify ownership of movable property. This definition underpins Sections 481–489. Unlike a trade mark (which denotes trade origin), a property mark denotes ownership of specific movable goods.

sections.heading: Using a false trade mark
sections.text: [Using a false trade mark.] Repealed by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 (43 of 1958), s. 135 and Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).
sections.key_principle: Originally penalised the use of a false trade mark. Repealed and superseded by the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, and subsequently the Trade Marks Act, 1999.

footnotes.text: The word "Trade" omitted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Relating to Documents and to Property Marks

sections.heading: Using a false property mark
sections.text: Whoever marks any movable property or goods or any case, package or other receptacle containing movable property or goods, or uses any case, package or other receptacle having any mark thereon, in a manner reasonably calculated to cause it to be believed that the property or goods so marked, or any property or goods contained in any such receptacle so marked, belong to a person to whom they do not belong, is said to use a false property mark.
ingredients: Marking movable property, goods, or a receptacle containing them; OR using a receptacle bearing a mark
In a manner reasonably calculated to cause a belief
That the property or goods belong to a person to whom they do not belong
sections.key_principle: Definition section — establishes what constitutes 'use of a false property mark'. The offence is complete on the act of marking or using a marked receptacle in a misleading manner; no actual deception of a specific person need be proved. Punishment is prescribed under Section 482. Amended by Act 4 of 1889 (substituted for original ss. 478–489) and further modified by Act 43 of 1958 (Trade and Merchandise Marks Act) which omitted all references to 'trade mark'.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 4 of 1889, s. 3, for the original heading and ss. 478 to 489.
The word 'Trade' omitted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

sections.heading: Punishment for using a false property mark
sections.text: Whoever uses any false property mark shall, unless he proves that he acted without intent to defraud, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Punishment provision for Section 481. Introduces a reverse burden of proof — the accused must prove absence of intent to defraud; the prosecution need not prove fraudulent intent. The words 'any false trade mark or' were omitted by Act 43 of 1958 (w.e.f. 25-11-1959), confining the section to false property marks only.
sections.reverse_burden_note: Accused must prove he acted without intent to defraud.

footnotes.note_text: The words 'any false trade mark or' omitted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

sections.heading: Counterfeiting a property mark used by another
sections.text: Whoever counterfeits any property mark used by any other person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Targets the act of counterfeiting a property mark belonging to another person — i.e., making a mark so as to resemble or pass off as that person's genuine mark. Heavier than Section 482 (use of false mark) — reflects that actual counterfeiting involves greater moral culpability than merely using a mislabelled receptacle. The words 'trade mark or' were omitted by Act 43 of 1958 (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

footnotes.note_text: The words 'trade mark or' omitted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

sections.heading: Counterfeiting a mark used by a public servant
sections.text: Whoever counterfeits any property mark used by a public servant, or any mark used by a public servant to denote that any property has been manufactured by a particular person or at a particular time or place, or that the property is of a particular quality or has passed through a particular office, or that it is entitled to any exemption, or uses as genuine any such mark knowing the same to be counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Counterfeiting any property mark used by a public servant; OR any official mark denoting manufacturer, time, place, quality, office, or exemption
OR using as genuine any such official mark knowing it to be counterfeit
sections.key_principle: Aggravated provision — counterfeiting marks of the State or a public servant carries a mandatory fine in addition to imprisonment (unlike Sections 482 and 483 where fine is alternative). Reflects the heightened public harm in subverting official certification systems. Two-limb offence: making the counterfeit mark, or knowingly using it as genuine.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.heading: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark
sections.text: Whoever makes or has in his possession any die, plate or other instrument for the purpose of counterfeiting a property mark, or has in his possession a property mark for the purpose of denoting that any goods belong to a person to whom they do not belong, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Makes or possesses any die, plate or other instrument for the purpose of counterfeiting a property mark; OR
Possesses a property mark for the purpose of falsely attributing goods to a person to whom they do not belong
sections.key_principle: Preparatory offence — punishes the making or possession of counterfeiting tools before any actual counterfeiting is done. Fine is alternative (not mandatory as in Section 484). Substituted in its entirety by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959) to remove references to trade mark instruments.
sections.amendment_note: Section 485 substituted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch., for the original s. 485 (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

sections.heading: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark
sections.text: Whoever sells, or exposes, or has in possession for sale, any goods or things with a counterfeit property mark affixed to or impressed upon the same or to or upon any case, package or other receptacle in which such goods are contained, shall, unless he proves (a) that, having taken all reasonable precautions against committing an offence against this section, he had at the time of the commission of the alleged offence no reason to suspect the genuineness of the mark, and (b) that, on demand made by or on behalf of the prosecutor, he gave all the information in his power with respect to the persons from whom he obtained such goods or things, or (c) that otherwise he had acted innocently, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Selling, exposing for sale, or possessing for sale any goods or things
Bearing a counterfeit property mark affixed or impressed on the goods or their receptacle
sections.key_principle: Targets commercial dealing in goods bearing counterfeit property marks. Provides three statutory defences available to the accused — any one of (a), (b), or (c) is sufficient to escape punishment. Defence (a): precautions taken + no reason to suspect. Defence (b): full cooperation with prosecutor's inquiry. Defence (c): general innocent dealing. The opening words were substituted by Act 43 of 1958 to omit reference to trade mark.
sections.reverse_burden_note: Accused must prove one of three statutory defences: (a) precaution and no reason to suspect; (b) cooperation with inquiry; or (c) innocent dealing.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 43 of 1958, s. 135 and the Sch., for certain words (w.e.f. 25-11-1959).

sections.heading: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods
sections.text: Whoever makes any false mark upon any case, package or other receptacle containing goods, in a manner reasonably calculated to cause any public servant or any other person to believe that such receptacle contains goods which it does not contain or that it does not contain goods which it does contain, or that the goods contained in such receptacle are of a nature or quality different from the real nature or quality thereof, shall, unless he proves that he acted without intent to defraud, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Making a false mark upon any case, package or other receptacle containing goods
In a manner reasonably calculated to deceive a public servant or any other person
As to the contents, presence, or nature/quality of goods in the receptacle
sections.key_principle: Targets mislabelling of containers — covers three categories of deception: false representation of contents present, false representation of contents absent, and false representation as to nature or quality of goods. Reverse burden — accused must prove absence of intent to defraud. Higher maximum than Section 482 (3 years vs 1 year), reflecting that mislabelling receptacles can facilitate customs fraud, quality fraud, and public procurement fraud.
sections.reverse_burden_note: Accused must prove he acted without intent to defraud.

sections.heading: Punishment for making use of any such false mark
sections.text: Whoever makes use of any such false mark in any manner prohibited by the last foregoing section shall, unless he proves that he acted without intent to defraud, be punished as if he had committed an offence against that section.
sections.key_principle: Extension of Section 487 — the user of a false mark on a receptacle (as prohibited by s. 487) is punished identically to the person who made the mark. 'Last foregoing section' refers to Section 487. Reverse burden on accused to prove absence of intent to defraud. Bridges the gap between makers and users of false receptacle marks.
sections.reverse_burden_note: Accused must prove he acted without intent to defraud.

punishment_options.condition: Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both — unless accused proves no intent to defraud

sections.heading: Tampering with property mark with intent to cause injury
sections.text: Whoever removes, destroys, defaces or adds to any property mark, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Removes, destroys, defaces or adds to any property mark
Intending to cause injury to any person; OR knowing it to be likely to cause injury to any person
sections.key_principle: Covers four modes of tampering: removal, destruction, defacement, and addition. Unlike Sections 481–488 which address false marking/counterfeiting, this section targets interference with existing genuine marks. Intent or knowledge of likely injury is the mens rea — not fraudulent intent. Broader protection — extends to any injury, not just financial. Closing section of the original ss. 478–489 block substituted by Act 4 of 1889.

mens_rea_modes.description: Intention to cause injury to any person by tampering with the mark
Knowledge that the tampering is likely to cause injury to any person

sections.heading: Counterfeiting currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.text: Whoever counterfeits, or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting, any currency-note or bank-note, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Counterfeiting any currency-note or bank-note; OR
Knowingly performing any part of the process of counterfeiting such note
sections.key_principle: Most serious of the currency counterfeiting offences — carries imprisonment for life as maximum, reflecting the grave threat to monetary systems and the national economy. The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955. 'Knowingly performs any part of the process' ensures that all participants in the counterfeiting chain (printers, engravers, paper suppliers with knowledge) are covered. Inserted as a distinct chapter by Act 12 of 1899.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: For the purposes of this section and of sections 489B, 489C, 489D and 489E, the expression 'bank-note' means a promissory note or engagement for the payment of money to bearer on demand issued by any person carrying on the business of banking in any part of the world, or issued by or under the authority of any State or Sovereign Power, and intended to be used as equivalent to, or as a substitute for money.
explanations.plain_language: A 'bank-note' for these sections is any bearer-on-demand instrument issued by a bank or State anywhere in the world and intended to function as money — the definition is intentionally international in scope.

sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956). Reference to Section 489E added by Act 35 of 1950.

footnotes.note_text: Added by Act 12 of 1899, s. 2.
Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).
Substituted by Act 35 of 1950, s. 3 and the Second Sch., for '489C and 489D'.

sections.heading: Using as genuine, forged or counterfeit currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.text: Whoever sells to, or buys or receives from, any other person, or otherwise traffics in or uses as genuine, any forged or counterfeit currency-note or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be forged or counterfeit, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Sells to, or buys or receives from any other person, or otherwise traffics in, any forged or counterfeit currency-note or bank-note; OR uses such note as genuine
Knowing or having reason to believe the note to be forged or counterfeit
sections.key_principle: Covers the entire distribution chain — selling, buying, receiving, general trafficking, and passing off as genuine. The mental element is 'knowing or having reason to believe' — constructive knowledge (reason to believe) suffices; actual knowledge is not required. Same maximum punishment as Section 489A (life imprisonment), reflecting that circulation of counterfeit currency is equally harmful as its manufacture. Fine is mandatory.

mens_rea_modes.description: Actual knowledge that the note is forged or counterfeit
Having reason to believe the note is forged or counterfeit (constructive knowledge)

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Possession of forged or counterfeit currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.text: Whoever has in his possession any forged or counterfeit currency-note or bank-note, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be forged or counterfeit and intending to use the same as genuine or that it may be used as genuine, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Possession of any forged or counterfeit currency-note or bank-note
Knowing or having reason to believe it to be forged or counterfeit
Intending to use it as genuine or that it may be used as genuine
sections.key_principle: Lower maximum than Sections 489A and 489B (7 years vs 10 years/life) — reflects that mere possession is less harmful than manufacture or active circulation. However, two mental elements must both be present: (i) knowledge/reason to believe the note is counterfeit, and (ii) intent to use or allow use as genuine. Fine is alternative, not mandatory. Absence of either mental element is a defence.

mens_rea_modes.description: Knowledge or reason to believe the note is forged/counterfeit
Intention to use as genuine or that it may be used as genuine

sections.heading: Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.text: Whoever makes, or performs any part of the process of making, or buys or sells or disposes of, or has in his possession, any machinery, instrument or material for the purpose of being used, or knowing or having reason to believe that it is intended to be used, for forging or counterfeiting any currency-note or bank-note, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Makes, performs any part of making, buys, sells, disposes of, or possesses
Any machinery, instrument or material
For the purpose of being used for forging or counterfeiting currency-notes or bank-notes; OR knowing or having reason to believe it is intended to be so used
sections.key_principle: Preparatory counterfeiting offence — targets the infrastructure of currency counterfeiting (printing presses, plates, special paper, inks). Same maximum punishment as Section 489A (life imprisonment + mandatory fine) — reflecting that the tools of counterfeiting are as dangerous as the act itself. Covers the entire supply chain: makers, buyers, sellers, disposers, and possessors of counterfeiting instruments. Fine is mandatory.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation for life' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes
sections.text: Whoever makes, or causes to be made, or uses for any purpose whatsoever, or delivers to any person, any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency-note or bank-note shall be punished with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees.

subsections.heading: Making or using documents resembling currency
subsections.text: Whoever makes, or causes to be made, or uses for any purpose whatsoever, or delivers to any person, any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency-note or bank-note shall be punished with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees.

subsections.heading: Refusal to disclose printer's identity
subsections.text: If any person, whose name appears on a document the making of which is an offence under sub-section (1), refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police-officer on being so required the name and address of the person by whom it was printed or otherwise made, he shall be punished with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees.

punishment.note: Fine only — no imprisonment; applies to named persons who refuse to identify the printer

subsections.heading: Presumption against named person
subsections.text: Where the name of any person appears on any document in respect of which any person is charged with an offence under sub-section (1) or on any other document used or distributed in connection with that document it may, until the contrary is proved, be presumed that that person caused the document to be made.
subsections.key_principle: Statutory presumption — a person whose name appears on the offending document is presumed to have caused it to be made, until the contrary is proved. Shifts the burden of rebuttal to the named person.

sections.key_principle: Minor offence — covers currency-lookalike documents (advertising novelty notes, promotional material resembling bank-notes) and is punishable only by fine. Far less severe than Sections 489A–D which address actual counterfeiting. Inserted by Act 6 of 1943 to address wartime currency mimicry.

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 6 of 1943, s. 2.

chapters.chapter_title: Of the Criminal Breach of Contracts of Service

sections.heading: Breach of contract of service during voyage or journey
sections.text: [Breach of contract of service during voyage or journey.] Rep. by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (3 of 1925), s. 2 and Sch.
sections.key_principle: Repealed in its entirety by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (Act 3 of 1925). No longer operative.
sections.repealed_by: Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (Act 3 of 1925), s. 2 and Schedule

sections.heading: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person
sections.text: Whoever, being bound by a lawful contract to attend on or to supply the wants of any person who, by reason of youth, or of unsoundness of mind, or of a disease or bodily weakness, is helpless or incapable of providing for his own safety or of supplying his own wants, voluntarily omits so to do, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees, or with both.
ingredients: Being bound by a lawful contract to attend on or supply wants of a person
That person is helpless due to youth, unsoundness of mind, disease, or bodily weakness
Voluntary omission to perform the contractual duty
sections.key_principle: Unique surviving provision of Chapter XIX — imposes criminal liability for breach of a care contract where the beneficiary is a vulnerable person incapable of self-care. Requires: (i) a lawful contract of care/attendance, (ii) vulnerability of the protected person (youth, mental incapacity, disease, or bodily weakness), and (iii) voluntary omission. Maximum fine is rupees two hundred (fixed amount — not the general 'such fine as the court thinks fit'). Short maximum imprisonment (3 months) reflects the contractual rather than malicious nature of the wrong.
protected_categories: Persons helpless by reason of youth

sections.heading: Breach of contract to serve at distant place to which servant is conveyed at master's expense
sections.text: [Breach of contract to serve at distant place to which servant is conveyed at master's expense.] Rep. by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (3 of 1925), s. 2 and Sch.
sections.key_principle: Repealed in its entirety by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (Act 3 of 1925). No longer operative.
sections.repealed_by: Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (Act 3 of 1925), s. 2 and Schedule

chapters.chapter_title: Of Offences Relating to Marriage

sections.heading: Cohabitation caused by a man deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage
sections.text: Every man who by deceit causes any woman who is not lawfully married to him to believe that she is lawfully married to him and to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: By deceit
Causes a woman (who is not lawfully married to him) to believe she is lawfully married to him
Causes her to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief
sections.key_principle: Gender-specific offence — applies only to men. The core wrong is inducing a false belief of valid marriage and then exploiting that belief for cohabitation or sexual intercourse. Distinguished from Section 496 (fraudulent marriage ceremony) — this section targets belief-based deceit without necessarily involving a ceremony. Fine is mandatory ('shall also be liable to fine').

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.heading: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife
sections.text: Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Having a husband or wife still living
Contracting a marriage
Which is void by reason of taking place during the life of such husband or wife (bigamy)
sections.key_principle: Bigamy provision. Gender-neutral — applies to both husbands and wives. The marriage must be void under law by reason of the existing spouse being alive. Fine is mandatory. Two statutory exceptions protect those who remarry after a court declaration of voidance, or after seven continuous years of absence of the earlier spouse (without knowledge of being alive), subject to full disclosure to the new spouse before marriage.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

exceptions.text: Does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction.
exceptions.key_principle: Court-declared voidance of the prior marriage is a complete defence to bigamy.

exceptions.text: Nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time — provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge.
exceptions.key_principle: Seven-year continuous absence + no knowledge of being alive = defence to bigamy, but full disclosure to new spouse before marriage is a mandatory precondition.

sections.heading: Same offence with concealment of former marriage from person with whom subsequent marriage is contracted
sections.text: Whoever commits the offence defined in the last preceding section having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Commits the offence of bigamy under Section 494
And additionally conceals from the new spouse the fact of the existing prior marriage
sections.key_principle: Aggravated bigamy — Section 494 + concealment of the prior marriage from the new spouse. Higher maximum imprisonment (10 years) than base Section 494 (7 years) reflects the additional wrong of deceiving the new spouse. Fine remains mandatory. The concealment must be of the fact of the prior marriage — any active hiding or withholding of this information qualifies.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.heading: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage
sections.text: Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Goes through the ceremony of being married
Knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married
Done dishonestly or with fraudulent intention
sections.key_principle: Distinguished from Section 493 (no ceremony necessary — just deceit inducing belief) and Section 494 (actual bigamous marriage). This section targets sham marriages — ceremonies performed with knowledge of legal invalidity, motivated by dishonest or fraudulent purpose. The invalidity may arise from any legal defect (existing spouse alive, prohibited relationship, non-compliance with formalities). Fine is mandatory.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.heading: Adultery
sections.text: Whoever has sexual intercourse with a person who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of another man, without the consent or connivance of that man, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, is guilty of the offence of adultery, and shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both. In such case the wife shall not be punishable as an abettor.
sections.key_principle: Note: Section 497 was struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of India in Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) 2 SCC 189 — it was held to violate Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution. The section is therefore no longer operative in law. Historically: gender-specific provision that only penalised the man; the wife was expressly excluded as an abettor. The husband's consent or connivance was a complete defence.
sections.constitutional_status: Struck down as unconstitutional — Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) 2 SCC 189. No longer operative.
ingredients: Sexual intercourse with a woman
Who is and whom the accused knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of another man
Without the consent or connivance of the husband
The intercourse does not amount to rape

sections.heading: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman
sections.text: Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, from that man, or from any person having the care of her on behalf of that man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Takes or entices away, OR conceals or detains, any woman
Who is (and whom the accused knows or has reason to believe to be) the wife of another man
From that man or from any person having her care on his behalf
With intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person
sections.key_principle: Four modes of actus reus: taking, enticing, concealing, or detaining. The specific intent is illicit intercourse — general motive of separation without this intent does not suffice. Knowledge or reason to believe she is a married woman is required. Distinguished from Section 497 (adultery) — this section protects the matrimonial household by penalising the person who facilitates the illicit liaison, not necessarily the person committing it.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Cruelty by Husband or Relatives of Husband

sections.heading: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty
sections.text: Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.
ingredients: Being the husband or relative of the husband of a woman
Subjecting such woman to cruelty (as defined in the Explanation)
sections.key_principle: Inserted by Act 46 of 1983 in response to rising incidents of dowry-related violence and bride burning. Cognizable and non-bailable offence. Fine is mandatory ('shall also be liable to fine'). The definition of 'cruelty' in the Explanation is two-limbed: (a) physical/mental wilful conduct likely to drive her to suicide or cause grave injury; and (b) harassment for unlawful property demands. Frequently invoked alongside Sections 304B (dowry death) and Section 406 (criminal breach of trust) in matrimonial cases.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: For the purposes of this section, 'cruelty' means — (a) any wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.
explanations.plain_language: Cruelty has two branches: (a) wilful conduct seriously endangering mental or physical health, or likely to drive the woman to suicide; and (b) harassment to coerce unlawful property/dowry demands from her or her family.

punishment_options.condition: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

footnotes.note_text: Inserted by Act 46 of 1983, s. 2.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Defamation

sections.heading: Defamation
sections.text: Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.
ingredients: By words (spoken or intended to be read), signs, or visible representations
Makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person
With intent to harm, or knowing/having reason to believe the imputation will harm, the reputation of such person
sections.key_principle: Definition section — covers four modes: spoken words, written/printed words (intended to be read), signs, and visible representations (pictures, cartoons, gestures). Both making and publishing are covered. Mental element: intent to harm reputation, or knowledge/reason to believe harm to reputation will result. Section 500 prescribes punishment. Ten exceptions protect constitutionally legitimate speech (truth for public good, fair comment, public servant's conduct, etc.).

explanations.label: Explanation 1
explanations.text: It may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person, if the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of his family or other near relatives.
explanations.plain_language: Defamation of a deceased person is possible if the imputation would have harmed their living reputation and is intended to hurt their family.

explanations.label: Explanation 2
explanations.text: It may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such.
explanations.plain_language: Defamation can be of a legal entity (company, association) or a group of persons — not just individuals.

explanations.label: Explanation 3
