explanations.text: An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation.
explanations.plain_language: Irony and rhetorical alternatives ('He never stole B's watch') can constitute defamation — the form of words does not determine whether the imputation is defamatory.

explanations.label: Explanation 4
explanations.text: No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or indirectly, in the estimation of others, lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person, or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person, or causes it to be believed that the body of that person is in a loathsome state, or in a state generally considered as disgraceful.
explanations.plain_language: An imputation harms reputation only if it lowers one or more of: moral/intellectual character, caste/professional character, credit, or bodily reputation (loathsome/disgraceful condition).

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A says — 'Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch'; intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
illustrations.key_principle: Ironical or indirect imputations are caught — the words on their face may be complimentary but their intended meaning is defamatory.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A is asked who stole B's watch. A points to Z, intending to cause it to be believed that Z stole B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
illustrations.key_principle: Defamation by sign or gesture — pointing as a non-verbal imputation of theft.

illustrations.label: Illustration (c)
illustrations.text: A draws a picture of Z running away with B's watch, intending it to be believed that Z stole B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
illustrations.key_principle: Defamation by visible representation — a drawing or cartoon that imputes a crime is defamatory.

exceptions.heading: Imputation of truth which public good requires to be made or published
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to impute anything which is true concerning any person, if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published. Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.

exceptions.heading: Public conduct of public servants
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the conduct of a public servant in the discharge of his public functions, or respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.

exceptions.heading: Conduct of any person touching any public question
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the conduct of any person touching any public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.

exceptions.heading: Publication of reports of proceedings of courts
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to publish a substantially true report of the proceedings of a Court of Justice, or of the result of any such proceedings.
exceptions.explanation: A Justice of the Peace or other officer holding an enquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in a Court of Justice, is a Court within the meaning of this section.

exceptions.heading: Merits of case decided in Court or conduct of witnesses and others concerned
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court of Justice, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.

exceptions.heading: Merits of public performance
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further.
exceptions.explanation: A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public.

exceptions.heading: Censure passed in good faith by person having lawful authority over another
exceptions.text: It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.

exceptions.heading: Accusation preferred in good faith to authorised person
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to prefer in good faith an accusation against any person to any of those who have lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.

exceptions.heading: Imputation made in good faith by person for protection of his or other's interests
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to make an imputation on the character of another provided that the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.

exceptions.heading: Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good
exceptions.text: It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good.

sections.heading: Punishment for defamation
sections.text: Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Punishment provision for defamation as defined in Section 499. Simple imprisonment only — rigorous imprisonment is not available. Note: Section 499/500 has been challenged as unconstitutional for criminalising speech, but the Supreme Court upheld its constitutional validity in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) 7 SCC 221.

sections.heading: Printing or engraving matter known to be defamatory
sections.text: Whoever prints or engraves any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory of any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Printing or engraving any matter
Knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory of any person
sections.key_principle: Extends liability for defamation to printers and engravers who have knowledge (actual or constructive) of the defamatory nature of the matter they print. Mental element: knowing OR having good reason to believe — the standard is 'good reason to believe', which is more exacting than 'reason to believe' (as in Section 26 IPC). Same punishment as Section 500.

sections.heading: Sale of printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter
sections.text: Whoever sells or offers for sale any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing that it contains such matter, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Selling or offering for sale any printed or engraved substance
Containing defamatory matter
Knowing that it contains such matter
sections.key_principle: Extends the defamation chain to sellers and distributors of defamatory printed/engraved material. Mental element is actual knowledge — 'knowing that it contains such matter' (stricter than s. 501 which adds 'good reason to believe'). Covers both completed sales and mere offers to sell. Same punishment as Sections 500 and 501.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult and Annoyance

sections.heading: Criminal intimidation
sections.text: Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.
ingredients: Threatens another with injury to: (i) person, (ii) reputation, or (iii) property of the victim or anyone in whom the victim is interested

With intent to: (a) cause alarm to that person; OR (b) cause that person to do any act not legally bound to do; OR (c) cause that person to omit any act legally entitled to do — as a means of avoiding the threat
sections.key_principle: Definition section — covers threats targeting the victim's person, reputation, property, or the same of anyone the victim cares about (family, friends). Three distinct intents are specified. 'Injury' in this section means legally recognised wrong — threats of financial, reputational, or bodily harm. The Explanation extends the section to threats against the reputation of deceased persons in whom the victim is interested. Punishment under Section 506.

explanations.label: Explanation
explanations.text: A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section.
explanations.plain_language: Threatening to harm the posthumous reputation of a deceased person dear to the victim falls within criminal intimidation.

illustrations.label: Illustration
illustrations.text: A, for the purpose of inducing B to desist from prosecuting a civil suit, threatens to burn B's house. A is guilty of criminal intimidation.
illustrations.key_principle: Threat to property (arson) used as coercion to abandon legal rights — classic criminal intimidation.

sections.heading: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace
sections.text: Whoever intentionally insults, and thereby gives provocation to any person, intending or knowing it to be likely that such provocation will cause him to break the public peace, or to commit any other offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Intentionally insults another
Thereby giving provocation to that person
Intending or knowing it to be likely that the provocation will cause that person to: (a) break the public peace; OR (b) commit any other offence
sections.key_principle: Two-step mental element: (i) intentional insult (not mere accidental rudeness), and (ii) intent or knowledge that the resulting provocation will lead to a breach of peace or other offence. Distinguishes lawful offensive speech from speech calculated to trigger violence or criminal retaliation. The actual breach of peace need not occur — the intent or likely consequence suffices.

sections.heading: Statements conducing to public mischief
sections.text: Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement, rumour or report — (a) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman in the Army, Navy or Air Force of India to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty as such; or (b) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public, or to any section of the public whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against the public tranquility; or (c) with intent to incite, or which is likely to incite, any class or community of persons to commit any offence against any other class or community, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

subsections.heading: Main offence — statements conducing to public mischief

clauses.text: With intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman in the Army, Navy or Air Force of India to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty as such.

With intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public, or to any section of the public whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against the public tranquility.
With intent to incite, or which is likely to incite, any class or community of persons to commit any offence against any other class or community.

subsections.heading: Statements creating or promoting enmity, hatred or ill-will between classes
subsections.text: Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement or report containing rumour or alarming news with intent to create or promote, or which is likely to create or promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community or any other ground whatsoever, feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

subsections.heading: Offence under sub-section (2) committed in place of worship
subsections.text: Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (2) in any place of worship or in any assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

punishment.fine: Mandatory — 'shall also be liable to fine'

sections.key_principle: Section 505 was substituted by Act 4 of 1898 and further amended by Act 35 of 1969 (which added sub-sections (2) and (3) and renumbered the original as sub-section (1)). Three-tier structure: (1) general public mischief statements; (2) communal/class hatred statements; (3) aggravated offence in places of worship (5-year maximum + mandatory fine). Covers both intent-based and likely-consequence-based offences — prosecution need not always prove specific intent. Exception: good faith and reasonable grounds for believing the statement to be true is a defence.

exceptions.label: Exception
exceptions.text: It does not amount to an offence, within the meaning of this section, when the person making, publishing or circulating any such statement, rumour or report, has reasonable grounds for believing that such statement, rumour or report is true and makes, publishes or circulates it in good faith and without any such intent as aforesaid.
exceptions.key_principle: Good faith + reasonable grounds to believe truth + absence of the requisite intent = complete defence.

sections.amendment_note: Section 505 renumbered as sub-section (1) by Act 35 of 1969, s. 3. Sub-sections (2) and (3) inserted by the same Act. References to 'sailor or airman', 'Navy or Air Force', and 'of India' substituted or added by earlier amendments. Maximum punishment raised from two years to three years by Act 41 of 1961.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 4 of 1898, s. 6, for the original s. 505.
Section 505 re-numbered as sub-section (1) of that section by Act 35 of 1969, s. 3.
Substituted by Act 41 of 1961, s. 4, for 'two years'.
Sub-sections (2) and (3) inserted by Act 35 of 1969, s. 3.

sections.heading: Punishment for criminal intimidation
sections.text: Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both; and if the threat be to cause death or grievous hurt, or to cause the destruction of any property by fire, or to cause an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or to impute unchastity to a woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both.
sections.key_principle: Two-tier punishment provision for criminal intimidation defined in Section 503. Base offence: up to 2 years. Aggravated offence (if the threat is of death, grievous hurt, arson, serious offences punishable with death/life/7-year imprisonment, or imputation of unchastity to a woman): up to 7 years. The aggravated limb targets threats that are most alarming in nature and most likely to coerce compliance.

punishment_options.condition: Up to two years, or fine, or both

Up to seven years, or fine, or both — when threat is of: death, grievous hurt, destruction of property by fire, offence punishable with death/life/7-year imprisonment, or imputation of unchastity to a woman

sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation' (w.e.f. 1-1-1956).

sections.heading: Criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication
sections.text: Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication, or having taken precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person from whom the threat comes, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to the punishment provided for the offence by the last preceding section.
ingredients: Commits the offence of criminal intimidation (Section 503)
By an anonymous communication; OR having taken precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person from whom the threat comes
sections.key_principle: Additional punishment — the two years under this section is imposed in addition to (not instead of) the punishment under Section 506. Anonymity or deliberate concealment of identity aggravates the intimidation because it frustrates legal recourse and heightens alarm. The precaution need not succeed — taking the precaution to conceal identity is sufficient.

punishment_options.condition: Up to two years — in addition to the punishment under Section 506

sections.heading: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of the Divine displeasure
sections.text: Whoever voluntarily causes or attempts to cause any person to do anything which that person is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do anything which he is legally entitled to do, by inducing or attempting to induce that person to believe that he or any person in whom he is interested will become or will be rendered by some act of the offender an object of Divine displeasure if he does not do the thing which it is the object of the offender to cause him to do, or if he does the thing which it is the object of the offender to cause him to omit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.
ingredients: Voluntarily causes or attempts to cause any person to do any act not legally bound to do, or omit any act legally entitled to do
By inducing or attempting to induce that person to believe that he or any person in whom he is interested will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure
If he does not comply with what the offender wants
sections.key_principle: Targets religious coercion — using the threat of Divine displeasure (curses, sitting dhurna with a religious connotation, threats of spiritual harm) to compel or prevent a legally free act. Covers both completed inducement and mere attempts. The belief of Divine displeasure may be induced against the victim or any person in whom the victim is interested (family, associates). Religious sincerity of the offender is immaterial.

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A sits dhurna at Z's door with the intention of causing it to be believed that, by so sitting, he renders Z an object of Divine displeasure. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Sitting dhurna with religious coercive intent — even a passive act can constitute this offence if the intent is to induce belief in Divine displeasure.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A threatens Z that, unless Z performs a certain act, A will kill one of A's own children, under such circumstances that the killing would be believed to render Z an object of Divine displeasure. A has committed the offence defined in this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Self-inflicted religious threat — threatening action against oneself to trigger belief that the victim will incur Divine wrath is equally caught.

sections.heading: Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman
sections.text: Whoever, intending to insult the modesty of any woman, utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object, intending that such word or sound shall be heard, or that such gesture or object shall be seen, by such woman, or intrudes upon the privacy of such woman, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also with fine.
ingredients: Intending to insult the modesty of any woman
Utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object — intending it to be heard or seen by such woman; OR
Intrudes upon the privacy of such woman
sections.key_principle: Gender-specific protective provision. Four modes: (i) words/sounds intended to be heard, (ii) gestures intended to be seen, (iii) exhibiting objects intended to be seen, and (iv) intrusion upon privacy. Intent to insult modesty is the essential mens rea. Punishment amended by Act 13 of 2013 — enhanced from 1 year (alternative fine) to 3 years simple imprisonment with mandatory fine (w.e.f. 3-2-2013). The amendment reflects the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013 (Nirbhaya Act) response to heightened concern about offences against women.
sections.amendment_note: Punishment substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 10, for the earlier provision of simple imprisonment up to one year or fine or both (w.e.f. 3-2-2013). Current punishment is 3 years simple imprisonment with mandatory fine.

footnotes.note_text: Substituted by Act 13 of 2013, s. 10, for 'shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both' (w.e.f. 3-2-2013).

sections.heading: Misconduct in public by a drunken person
sections.text: Whoever, in a state of intoxication, appears in any public place, or in any place which it is a trespass in him to enter, and there conducts himself in such a manner as to cause annoyance to any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to twenty-four hours, or with fine which may extend to ten rupees, or with both.
ingredients: In a state of intoxication
Appears in any public place, OR any place which it is a trespass for him to enter
Conducts himself in a manner as to cause annoyance to any person
sections.key_principle: Minor public order offence — lightest punishment in Chapter XXII (24 hours and/or Rs. 10 fine). Simple imprisonment only. Two-fold location requirement: public places, or places the person has no right to enter even sober (trespass). The conduct must cause actual annoyance to some person — mere intoxication in public without annoying conduct is insufficient. The nominal fine (Rs. 10) reflects the original 1860 valuation; the provision has not been updated for inflation.

chapters.chapter_title: Of Attempts to Commit Offences

sections.heading: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment
sections.text: Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Code with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall, where no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.
ingredients: Attempts to commit an offence punishable under the IPC with imprisonment for life or imprisonment; OR attempts to cause such an offence to be committed
In such attempt, does any act towards the commission of the offence
No express provision exists elsewhere in the Code for punishment of such attempt
sections.key_principle: Residual general attempt provision — applies only where the IPC does not elsewhere expressly prescribe punishment for the specific attempt (e.g., Section 307 for attempt to murder, Section 308 for attempt to commit culpable homicide already have express provisions; Section 511 fills the gap for all other cases). Three elements must coexist: (i) intent to commit the substantive offence, (ii) an overt act towards its commission, and (iii) failure to complete it. The punishment is half the maximum of the substantive offence — not a fixed term. Fine, if any, mirrors that of the substantive offence. Does not apply to offences punishable only by fine.
sections.scope_note: Section 511 is a residual/gap-filling provision. It does not apply where the Code already expressly punishes the attempt (e.g., Sections 121, 124, 125, 130, 131, 152, 153, 161, 165A, 196, 198, 200, 213, 239, 240, 241, 251, 385, 387, 389, 391, 393, 397, 398, 460, 307, 308, 309, 393 etc.).

punishment_options.type: Imprisonment of any description provided for the substantive offence
punishment_options.condition: Up to one-half of the imprisonment for life, or up to one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for the substantive offence
Such fine as is provided for the substantive offence

illustrations.label: Illustration (a)
illustrations.text: A makes an attempt to steal some jewels by breaking open a box, and finds after so opening the box, that there is no jewel in it. He has done an act towards the commission of theft, and therefore is guilty under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Impossibility of completing the offence due to absence of the subject matter does not negate the attempt — the act towards commission (breaking open the box) is sufficient for liability.

illustrations.label: Illustration (b)
illustrations.text: A makes an attempt to pick the pocket of Z by thrusting his hand into Z's pocket. A fails in the attempt in consequence of Z's having nothing in his pocket. A is guilty under this section.
illustrations.key_principle: Factual impossibility (empty pocket) is no defence to an attempt — the accused's act and intent are sufficient; the fortuitous absence of the object does not exculpate.

sections.amendment_note: The words 'imprisonment for life' were substituted for 'transportation' by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 1-1-1956). The punishment formula ('imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half...') was also substituted by the same Act for the earlier wording.
